observations.text: G2168 (thanksgiving withheld) co-occurs with knowledge (M15, G1097), honoring (M22, G1392), reasoning (M63, G1261), foolishness (M16, G0801), and heart (M47, G2588). Here thanksgiving's absence ('did not... give thanks') sits at the hinge of the moral collapse sequence: knowing God but failing to honor or thank Him leads to futile thinking, foolish hearts, and darkness — thanksgiving functions as the withheld response that should have followed true knowledge of God.

Here G2168 appears in a NEGATED clause ('did not... give thanks') — the surface sense is the absence/failure of the act rather than its performance, a notable contrast with John.6.23/1Thess.2.13 where the verb affirms the act. This negative-polarity usage marks Rom.1.21 as the cluster's clearest illustration of the negative pole: thanksgiving withheld as root of idolatrous decline.

G2168 is not itself tagged role-T3 here; the operation-tagged word 'became futile' (G3154, T3) applies to 'their thinking', an internal-state action rather than an interpersonal directed act toward a party.

Since G2168 is the subgroup's sole member strong, the cross-strong comparison this stage exists to perform collapses to a single-strong self-comparison: every occurrence -- whether epistolary-habitual, meal-blessing, exclamatory-nominal, negated, or personal/individual prayer-address -- shares the same root act (a verbal/enacted response of gratitude directed to God, occasionally to a human benefactor as in Rom.16.4) with no second lexeme to diverge from within this subgroup. The genuine internal variation is therefore register/context-driven (liturgical meal-formula vs. epistolary habit vs. individual prayer vs. negated failure) rather than lexical-sense divergence between two different words.

Rom.1.21 is the single occurrence across G2168's full list where the verb is negated ('did not... give thanks'), marking the negative pole of the strong's own range: rather than an enacted response of gratitude, it names the culpable withholding of that response despite prior knowledge of God, standing in structural contrast to every other occurrence (all of which depict thanksgiving actually performed). This is a difference visible only by scanning the strong's complete occurrence list rather than any single-verse reading.

In Rom.1.21 the negated form shows the reverse: the persons 'knew God' (a true perception) yet did not conclude that this knowledge required thanksgiving, revealing a fracture between correct perception and the judgement/response that should follow from it -- knowledge without gratitude, leading to futile thinking.

Across the verses thanksgiving overwhelmingly FOLLOWS a prior belief or perception (of grace given, faith proclaimed, deliverance accomplished, power exercised, prayer answered) -- it is a responsive act rather than a cause of belief. The one negative case (Rom.1.21) shows belief (knowing God) failing to produce the following act of thanks, confirming the normal sequence is belief-then-thanksgiving.

The evidence does not depict thanksgiving itself as a transformation of the person that could be reversible/irreversible; rather it shows a reversible failure-to-respond (Rom.1.21's withheld thanks leading to darkened hearts) alongside an ongoing, renewable practice (habitual thanksgiving) -- so the relevant contrast is presence versus withholding of the act on each occasion, not an irreversible change of state.

Thanksgiving's role reads as belonging to created design (it is the fitting response owed by a creature to its Creator/Benefactor for grace received, and its withholding is portrayed as culpable failure, Rom.1.21) that is now exercised within the fallen condition -- it is both what humanity was designed to render and what fallen humanity characteristically fails to render without renewal (as shown by the contrast between habitual apostolic thanksgiving and the idolaters' withheld thanks).

Thanksgiving is blocked or distorted where knowledge of God is present but not honored (Rom.1.21, leading to futile thinking and darkened hearts), and where it is co-opted for self-congratulation rather than genuine grace-acknowledgment (Luke.18.11's Pharisee). No adversarial-spirit interference is evidenced in these occurrences; the blocking factor shown is internal (pride, willful non-response to known truth).

In Rom.1.21, the person who knows God yet does not give him thanks is shown to have a heart that becomes 'darkened' and thinking that 'became futile' -- the inner-being state where the characteristic's opportunity is present (true knowledge of God) but not taken up is one of foolish, obscured, self-deceived cognition.

The relational scope is broad in principle (any person, believer or outsider, may give thanks, and thanks may be directed to God or to a human benefactor) but the evidence shows it functionally clustered among believers thanking God for one another and, in one negative case, withheld by those who knew God but refused to honor him -- excluding, by that refusal, themselves from the fitting response rather than the characteristic itself excluding any class of person.

The presence of thanksgiving in a person marks a rightly-functioning divine image -- one that perceives grace received and returns acknowledgment; its absence (Rom.1.21, knowing God yet not thanking him) marks the image obscured/darkened, since the capacity for grateful recognition of the Creator is treated as integral to what a rightly-functioning image-bearer does with true knowledge of God.

Thanksgiving, as the fitting creaturely response to God's giving nature, instantiates the aspect of the divine likeness that recognizes and rightly responds to grace/goodness received -- a relational-responsive aspect of the image (rightly ordered gratitude and dependence) rather than an aspect of God's own being shared substantively.

Where thanksgiving is present, it indicates the divine image is functioning rightly with respect to recognizing and honoring God as source of good; where absent despite true knowledge of God (Rom.1.21), it indicates the image is darkened/distorted, evidenced by the futile thinking and foolish heart that follow the withheld thanks.

No occurrence in the evidence depicts thanksgiving itself as a site of direct adversarial (satanic/demonic) attack or interference; the only 'blocking' pattern shown (Rom.1.21) attributes the failure to give thanks to human willful suppression of known truth, not to an adversarial spirit's action.

The pattern of engagement (speech/prayer consistently engaged; cognition/knowledge engaged where present as in Rom.1.21; body occasionally engaged as expressive vehicle, Luke.17.16) indicates thanksgiving's nature as fundamentally a mind-and-mouth response grounded in true perception of a benefactor's action, with the body serving only an expressive, non-essential role -- it is not primarily a bodily or purely emotional faculty-driven characteristic but a cognitive-verbal one.

Thanksgiving is compound in structure: it combines (1) recognition/perception of a favor or grace received, (2) an inward disposition of gratitude, and (3) an outward verbal (or bodily) enactment directed toward the benefactor -- the eu-charis root itself encodes the grace-recognition component fused with the responsive-return component.

The structural opposite of thanksgiving, as shown by its negation in Rom.1.21, is the willful withholding of due acknowledgment despite true knowledge -- ingratitude coupled with a darkened, futile mind; this is the inner-being reality that excludes thanksgiving even where the knowledge that should occasion it is present.

Adjacent characteristics co-occurring with thanksgiving across the verse evidence include: faith (M13, e.g. Rom.1.8, 2Thess.1.3), grace (M50, 1Cor.1.4), love (M51, 2Thess.1.3), prayer/remembrance (M42/M82, Col.1.3, Phil.1.3, 1Thess.1.2, Phlm.1.4, Eph.1.16), knowledge/honoring/heart (M15/M22/M47, Rom.1.21), and building up (M52, 1Cor.14.17) -- these recur frequently, especially the prayer/remembrance pairing in epistolary openings.

In Ps.38.12 and 2Sam.4.8 and Prov.29.10 the surface sense diverges from the neutral base gloss 'seek' because it participates in the idiom 'seek my life/his life' -- meaning to seek to kill, not merely to search for or desire. This idiomatic shift carries lethal hostile intent, contrasting against occurrences like 1Kgs.22.8 where the same root (H1875, related seeking root) denotes benign consultation of the Lord.

In Ps.38.12 those hostile to the psalmist (the party 'those who seek') initiate the seeking-operation, directed toward the psalmist's life/hurt -- an adversarial party seeking harm against the sole party present as target.

No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in Ps.38.12 alongside H1245 seeking; the other tagged words in the verse are role-T or non-cluster tags plus M47 (life), M24/M58 (hurt), M18 (ruin), M84 (meditate), M14 (treachery) -- checking against cluster scope, no additional M-code home-cluster overlap applies to H1245's own vantage beyond noting these are present but distinct; treat as no other M83-relevant relation to build on.

In Ps.10.4 darash (negated: 'does not seek') occupies the negative pole of the cluster's dual seeking-motif, paired with M08 pride and M58 wickedness in the same verse -- the wicked's pride is what suppresses the seeking-act, making darash's absence diagnostic of the wicked disposition.
In Ps.10.4, the seeking operation (negated) is attributed to 'the wicked' (party) with God as its withheld object -- the wicked initiates no such act toward God.
In John.11.56 an unspecified crowd/group (party, contextually pilgrims/authorities at the feast) initiates 'looking for' directed toward Jesus, debating whether he will come to the feast.
In John.11.56 'looking for Jesus' at the feast is a neutral searching-for-a-person sense, without hostile or ironic shading -- within the base gloss.

In John.11.56 M15 (dokeō, 'think') co-occurs with M83 (zēteō, 'looking for'). From M83's vantage, the crowd's active searching for Jesus is distinct from their separate act of opining/speculating (M15) about whether he will come -- the seeking is physical/locational while the thinking is deliberative, running in parallel rather than intersecting.
In John.11.56 'What do you think?' uses dokeō's ordinary interrogative-opinion sense, matching its base gloss with no notable divergence.
In John 20:15 Jesus asks Mary 'whom are you seeking' (zeteo) — plain literal search for a missing person, squarely within the base gloss, no divergence.

No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in this verse's role list at the home-cluster level; M03, M15, M72 appear on other words but are not this cluster's own home strongs, and no prior relational context exists to build on.

The operation 'seeking' is initiated by Mary (addressed as 'you') and directed toward the missing body of Jesus ('whom') — Jesus as questioner surfaces the operation, but the seeker-party is Mary, the sought object is Jesus/his body.

In Acts.10.19 and Acts.10.21, zeteo functions in its plain concrete sense 'looking for/seeking' -- the three men sent by Cornelius seeking Peter. This sits squarely within the base gloss with no distinguishing theological or hostile nuance, a straightforward physical search for a specific person.

M47 (Spirit) is present in Acts.10.19 as the divine speaker announcing that men are seeking Peter; the Spirit's speech-act and the men's seeking are related narratively (the Spirit reveals the seeking) but the Spirit itself does not seek -- it discloses and directs, a distinct characteristic from the seeking it reports.

M26 (reason/aitia, front-loaded) co-occurs with seeking in Acts.10.21 -- Peter confirms he is the one sought, then asks the reason (aitia) for the visitors' coming. The seeking (their prior action) prompts Peter's request for the reason behind it; reason-seeking here follows and explains the initial seeking rather than being enacted by it.
In Acts.10.19 the seeking/looking-for operation is initiated by the three men (party, T8) sent by Cornelius and directed toward Peter ('you'), reported to Peter by the Spirit.
In Acts.10.21 the seeking/looking-for operation is initiated by the men (party, T8) and directed toward Peter, who confirms himself as the one sought when he goes down to meet them.
In Acts.10.21 aitia is used in its plain practical sense 'reason/cause' (for the men's coming) -- sitting within the base gloss with no notable divergence.

In Acts.10.19 enthymeomai is used in its plain base sense 'ponder/consider carefully,' matching the tree's sole NT occurrence gloss with no additional divergence noted (this is its only NT occurrence, so no comparative pattern across multiple occurrences exists).

In Isa.58.2, Ezra.6.21, and 1Chr.28.9 'seek/worship' sits squarely within the base cultic-consultation/devotion sense of H1875, with no further distinguishing nuance beyond ordinary devotional seeking of God.

M15 (know), M36 (serve), M34 (whole/forever), M47 (heart/mind), M64 (plan), M06 (thought), M30/M59 (forsake), M18 (willing) all co-occur with H1875 in 1Chr.28.9; H1875's own vantage is that the verse pairs two mirrored uses of darash -- human seeking of God and divine searching of the heart -- forming the verse's relational spine that the other M-codes (serving, willing heart, forsaking) orbit as conditions or consequences of that mutual seeking.

In Matt.18.12 'search' sits within the base gloss of literal seeking (a shepherd seeking the lost sheep), extended metaphorically to pastoral care but not diverging structurally from the base sense of searching for something lost.
The man/shepherd (party) initiates the seeking-operation directed toward the one sheep that went astray.

M59/M60 (leave/abandon, G0863G) is present; the seeking-characteristic (M83, going in search of the lost sheep) stands in direct sequential/causal relation to the leaving-characteristic (the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine in order to seek) -- M83 is the purposeful continuation of the M59/M60 act.

baqash's idiom 'seek the life/soul' (e.g. Ps.38.12, 2Sam.4.8, Prov.29.10, Jer.4.30, Jer.11.21) consistently means 'seek to kill', a lethal-hostile-pursuit sense sharply diverging from the term's more neutral or devotional occurrences (e.g. 2Chr.15.13 'seek the Lord'), showing the root's moral valence is entirely determined by its grammatical object.

1Chr.28.9, Prov.11.27, and Job.39.8 all render darash as 'searches' but span three distinct registers: God searching all hearts (devotional-omniscient), a person searching for evil (moral-negative object), and a wild animal searching for pasture (literal/animal). This triad illustrates the verb's semantic elasticity across divine, moral, and mundane subjects within one surface form.

In Ps.10.4 the wicked's failure to seek God reveals his conclusion 'There is no God' -- the absence of inquiry is itself diagnostic of a settled unbelief; the characteristic here reveals a negative judgement about God's non-existence or irrelevance.

Across the verses both patterns occur: seeking/inquiring often precedes a resulting belief or outcome (e.g. 2Chr.14.7 'we have sought the Lord... he has given us peace', Ps.34.4 'I sought the Lord, and he answered me'), while elsewhere the failure or presence of seeking follows from an already-settled disposition (Ps.10.4's pride precedes and explains the non-seeking; 2Chr.12.14's evil is explained by not having set the heart to seek). The characteristic functions bidirectionally as both antecedent to and consequence of belief/judgement.

Seeking is blocked or nullified when the heart harbors idols or a stumbling block of iniquity even while outwardly consulting God -- Ezek.14.3, 14.7 explicitly describe men who 'have taken their idols into their hearts' yet 'come to a prophet to consult me' -- God declares he will not let himself be consulted (or will answer in judgment) in such cases; similarly pride (Ps.10.4 'in the pride of his face') suppresses seeking altogether.

The characteristic's presence marks a person as rightly oriented toward God in covenant fidelity, and its absence marks corruption or apostasy (Ps.10.4, 1Chr.10.14 'He did not seek guidance from the Lord... the Lord put him to death'); this indicates that the capacity to seek/inquire is part of humanity's created relational orientation toward God, and its exercise or neglect functions as a diagnostic marker of the divine image's proper functioning or its corruption in the person.

Where seeking is present in a person (2Chr.22.9 'sought the Lord with all his heart'), it indicates the divine image is functioning rightly in relational orientation toward God; where absent (Ps.10.4, 1Chr.10.14), it indicates a corrupted or suppressed image-bearing capacity, evidenced by pride and covenant unfaithfulness leading to death.

God's extension of the characteristic (his willingness to be sought/found) is shown as both conditional and responsive: conditional on genuine seeking ('If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever', 1Chr.28.9), yet also shown as gracious and unconditioned in Isa.65.1 ('I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me') -- God's self-disclosure as available to be inquired of exceeds strict conditionality, showing both a covenantal-conditional pattern and a gracious-responsive pattern.

The structural opposite of seeking is forsaking/neglecting -- explicitly named as the contrastive pole in 1Chr.28.9 ('if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever') and implied by negation in Ps.10.4 ('does not seek') and 1Chr.10.14 ('did not seek guidance') -- the inner-being reality that excludes seeking is self-sufficient neglect or active abandonment of the source that ought to be consulted.

At its edge, seeking excludes casual, passive, or half-hearted attention -- it resists mere outward performance without inner devotion (Ezek.14.3-7's idol-hearted consulters are the negative exemplar), and it excludes self-sufficiency/pride that renders inquiry unnecessary (Ps.10.4).

Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside seeking include 'heart/mind' (M47, frequently paired as the seat/manner of seeking, e.g. 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, Ps.119.2/10), 'trust' (M19, Ps.9.10, Isa.31.1), and 'forsake' (M30/M59, as antithetical pairing, Ps.9.10, 1Chr.28.9) -- these co-occur with notable frequency, showing seeking is characteristically bound to heart-language and its antithesis, forsaking.

Seeking consistently PRECEDES finding/being found and its resulting blessings: Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'; Isa.55.6 'Seek the Lord while he may be found'; 1Chr.28.9 'If you seek him, he will be found by you' -- the sequence is invariably seek-then-find, never the reverse, establishing seeking as the necessary antecedent condition.

The seek-then-find sequence is causal-conditional rather than merely correlational or developmental: the finding is explicitly conditioned upon the seeking ('IF you seek him, he WILL be found'), establishing a covenantal cause-and-effect relationship rather than a coincidental temporal succession.
"Do not be afraid", and the ground given each time.
Fear at the same kind of act, and asking him to go.
Fear when what is seen is taken for something else.
The fear root rendered "respect", toward people.
"Have no fear of them" and "with gentleness and respect": one word, two verses apart.
An apostle's fear for a church.
Fear in a man's considering, and fear met in a dream.
Fear leads to flight
Fear holds back from speaking: "Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli"; the servants "were afraid to tell him that the child was dead"; Elihu "was timid and afraid to declare my opinion"
Fear leads to wrong.
Fear is used against a person as a tool.

It is joined with turning from evil: "feared God and turned away from evil"; "fear the Lord, and turn away from evil"; "by the fear of the Lord one turns away from evil"; "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil"; "the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding"
It governs conduct toward the weak and toward others.
It is tested by what is withheld: "now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son"; and questioned: "Does Job fear God for no reason?"
Four occasions of blocked will:
The fallen face:
Vexation suffered
Strife among believers is traced to an inner source
Human anger is often shown with no inner word at all.
Asking once more, aware of the anger
Seen, and filled with fury; joy turned in a moment.
The burning verb, with and without ʾaph.
"Let not … be angry": said before God and before men.
Anger at another's honour, or at a work going forward.
God asks: "Why are you angry?" "Do you do well to be angry?"
The rival's provocation becomes Hannah's vexation.
Angry at a word that crossed what was expected; vexed and sullen.
The face that falls.
Where strife comes from.
Turning is considered, and it reaches back.
Death spoken of as sleep.
Death named inside a living person.
A body "as good as dead", and faith that considers it.
The heart and the soul as death comes near.
The fear of dying shapes what people do.
Swearing by the LORD's life and by the life of the one spoken to, as a bond.
The oath names what the LORD has done for the one who swears.
Life loathed.
"The land of the living" and the records of the living.
Life looked for in the wrong place, or refused.
What is called living.
The spirit against death while living.
The heart is where thoughts come from
Thoughts arise unbidden, often at night, and can be tied to revelation
The bed hosts both deliberate plotting and meditation on God.
Thoughts lodge and stay
What rises is shaped from outside: God writes on minds; he gives skill to devise; instruction and counsel form thought; minds can be blinded
yēṣer ("intention", "inclination") is the same word as the potter's thing formed, and as our frame.
God knows the inclination before it acts ("what they are inclined to do even today")
Thought as reckoning, i.e.
Thought as likening, i.e.
Thought as inner speech, often quoted as a sentence
hāgāh joins meditating, muttering and uttering in one word.
Reasoning within one heart and reasoning between people are one word (dialogizomai)
Thinking matures ("I thought like a child … I gave up childish ways")
Thought is creaturely and passing
God also speaks in his heart.
The path: arising → lodging → reckoning → devising → expression (tongue, lips, eyes) → action (hand, feet)
The same path runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet"; meditate day and night "so that you may be careful to do"
Thinking before speaking: "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out"
Responsibility sits from lodging onward.
Thought moves the body and emotions ("his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way"; "limping between two different opinions")
God thinks and plans, and his purpose stands over human plans
Thoughts are fully open to God and to Jesus.
False likeness: God likened to man ("you thought that I was one like yourself"); man likened to God ("I will make myself like the Most High"; "I am a god"; "you consider yourself a lion").
Faith reckons: Abraham "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead"
The inclination can be kept, directed and stayed.
Reckoning can be commanded and redirected: "consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God"; "think about these things"; "I consider that the sufferings … are not worth comparing"
Reckoning shapes conscience: a thing is "unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean"
Thought shaped by ease is contempt
Thinking alone can stall; the sanctuary changes what it sees
Night thoughts: revelation when God makes them known; alarm without that; a claimed night vision can be wrong
Inner reasoning becomes outward quarrel when it is shared and set on one's own standing
Imagination makes gods; the maker trusts his own creation
Flow 3: thoughts act back on the thinker.

People value and regard: "Are we not regarded by him as foreigners?" (Gen 31:15); "Let not my lord hold me guilty" (2Sa 19:19); "who have no regard for silver" (Isa 13:17); "there is no regard for man" (Isa 33:8); "they were considered reliable" (Neh 13:13); God's laws "would be regarded as a strange thing" (Hos 8:12); "The precious sons of Zion" "how they are regarded as earthen pots" (Lam 4:2); "will be counted as cursing" (Pro 27:14). And a person is regarded: "we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psa 44:22); "I am counted among those who go down to the pit" (Psa 88:4); Israel "not counting itself among the nations" (Num 23:9).

The looking-ahead words are used most often against another person. It is placed in the heart: "let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zec 7:10), "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zec 8:17). It is done together: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (Jer 18:18); "In Heshbon they planned disaster against her" (Jer 48:2); "they made plans to put him to death" (Joh 11:53), and Lazarus as well (Joh 12:10); "The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners" (Act 27:42). It is aimed at the righteous and the weak: "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psa 37:12); "who have planned to trip up my feet" (Psa 140:4). It hides behind a friendly word: "Come and let us meet together" "But they intended to do me harm" (Neh 6:2); Saul's bride-price, "Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (1Sa 18:25). It is pinned on the other side: "you and the Jews intend to rebel" (Neh 6:6). Another pleads against it: Esther "pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman" (Est 8:3; 9:24).

In the Greek the will is weighed against another's: "Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas" (Mar 15:15), after "do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?" (Joh 18:39); "when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him" (Act 19:30); "when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him" (Act 18:27); "they wished to set me at liberty" (Act 28:18), until the Jews objected; Diotrephes "stops those who want to and puts them out of the church" (3Jo 10); Paul "would have been glad to keep him with me" (Phm 13), and left the consent to Philemon.

Looking ahead weighs before it acts: a king "will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand" (Luk 14:31); "She considers a field and buys it" (Pro 31:16); "consider it, take counsel, and speak" (Judg 19:30). It plans without knowing: "on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix" (Act 27:12), "supposing that they had obtained their purpose" (Act 27:13), "they planned if possible to run the ship ashore" (Act 27:39). A plan carries a word: "Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say Yes, yes and No, no at the same time?" (2Co 1:17). Plans part people: "Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark" (Act 15:37); Joseph of Arimathea "had not consented to their decision and action" (Luk 23:51). And a plan can be for another's good: "because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom" (Dan 6:3).

Face A, fear felt before a threat or a person: afraid, feared, fear, fearful and exceedingly, with an enemy, a king, an army, a place, the sword or being found out as the object; the subject is the one who fears.
The woman of Tekoa's "the people have made me afraid" (2Sa 14:15) is part of a staged story (2Sa 14:2-3); the verse stays in face A as data only.

Who holds it, and toward whom: A people "a horror" to those who pass by and hiss; the prophet: "dismay has taken hold on me"; Eli's "heart trembled for the ark of God"; "I am afraid that … your thoughts will be led astray"
Forbidden and asked for, close together: "Have no fear of them" … "with gentleness and respect"; "do not fear what they fear" … "Let him be your fear"

Face B. Felt before God's presence, act or word, or a messenger (21 / 19 hits and verses; surfaces fear · afraid · terrified · terror · frightened · alarmed · trembled · tremble · trembling · awe): An angel; the voice from the cloud; the burning bush; Sinai; an act of judgment heard of; a word about judgment.

Face E. Awe, respect or reverence toward people (7 / 6 hits and verses; surfaces respect · respectful · respects · feared): The fear root rendered "respect": to rulers, masters, husbands, any who ask; Herod toward John.
Face P. Fear for another (4 / 4 hits and verses; surfaces afraid · fear): An apostle for a church; a tribune for a prisoner.

Face AH. Fear before Jesus' acts and person (19 / 17 hits and verses; surfaces afraid · fear · filled [with great fear] · terrified · frightened · startled · awe · greatly amazed): A storm stilled; walking on the sea; a man healed; the transfiguration; the risen Jesus; the passion foretold.
Forbidden and asked for, two verses apart: "Have no fear of them" … "with gentleness and respect".
The root ḥûl, "to twist, whirl", is rendered as birth: "the God who gave you birth" (Deu 32:18); "I was brought forth in iniquity" (Psa 51:5).

Fear aims at the hands: "Fear not, O Zion; let not your hands grow weak" (Zep 3:16); "they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, 'Their hands will drop from the work' ... But now, O God, strengthen my hands" (Neh 6:9).
H3372G "to fear" is rendered frighten: 2Ch 32:18, Neh 6:9.
The Greek fear words G5401 and G5399 is rendered respect: Rom 13:7, 1Pe 2:18, 3:15.
Face of aph (H0639), The face lifted in pride: The face/nose raised (Psa 10:4 ("In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him")). Pride is the nose held high (S, lexical).

ka'as (H3707/3708): provocation done (to God) · vexation borne (Hannah, Job) · sorrow that does good ("by sadness of face the heart is made glad") · the fool's vexation that kills him · God-induced vexation of the nations (Deu 32:16, 21; 1Sa 1:6–16; Job 6:2; 17:7; Ecc 7:3; Job 5:2; Eze 32:9). Done to another, it is provocation. Borne, it is suffering. Taken to heart, it can make the heart good (Ecc 7:3). The word follows the direction of the act (S/R).

It is felt in the body and the person: "Your wrath lies heavy upon me"; "There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation"; "So Cain was very angry, and his face fell"; "I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit"; "my spirit drinks their poison".
Form of anger, Intercession; asking him not to be angry; standing between (23 / 16 hits and verses; faces G, 2J, 3F, 4E; units 1–4).
Form of anger, Vexation and grief borne within (12 / 11 hits and verses; faces 3Y, 4X; units 3, 4).
Form of anger, The face that falls: Cain's anger; God's withheld anger (4 / 2 hits and verses; faces 4AE; units 4).

The one who carries it out: "Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger … but it is in his heart to destroy"; "you showed them no mercy"; "while I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster"; "you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven"; Saul judged for not carrying it out.

What the angry person does with it: Nehemiah: "I took counsel with myself"; Absalom "spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad"; Jacob's sons answered "deceitfully"; Samuel "cried to the Lord all night"; David "was afraid of the Lord that day"; Sanballat and Tobiah "plotted together"; Ahab "lay down on his bed and turned away his face"; Paul "reasoned in the synagogue".

One root, different things: ʾaph: "pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife"; ḥēmāh: wrath, "the venom of asps", "the heat of wine"; ʿebrāh: wrath and "arrogant pride"; zāʿam: anger and "How can I denounce"; zāʿap̄: Uzziah's anger and "Why are your faces downcast today?"; ʿāšan: "Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke" and "Why does your anger smoke"; kāʿas: provoking God and Hannah's "vexation"; thymos: God's "wrath" and Babylon's "passion"; paroxysmos: "a sharp disagreement" and "stir up one another to love".

What follows a person's anger is where the cases differ (v2, U1 §37): the face falls: "So Cain was very angry, and his face fell"; speech: "I must speak, that I may find relief"; counsel: "I took counsel with myself"; fear: "And David was afraid of the Lord that day"; mercy: "Not a man shall be put to death this day".
A person's anger leads to a face that falls; an eye that watches; a plot: "and his face fell"; "And Saul eyed David from that day on"; "And they all plotted together".
A person's anger leads to counsel, then open charge; reasoning: "I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles"; "So he reasoned in the synagogue".
A person responds to God's anger by plead: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak" (Gen 18:30).
Sequence in Gen 4:4–8: regard withheld → anger → face fallen → God reads the face and asks → sin at the door, "rule over it" → killing.

Sequence in 1Sa 1:6–18: provoked year by year → weeping, not eating → heart named by husband → "deeply distressed" (Hebrew bitter of soul) → heart-prayer, lips only → misread as drunk → self-explanation ("vexation") → blessing → eats, face no longer sad.
Sequence in 2Sa 13:20–39: "do not take this to heart" → the king very angry, no act → the brother's hatred waits two years → killing → the king's spirit longs for the killer.
Sequence in Isa 9:8–10:7: pride in rebuilding → struck → "did not turn" → leaders mislead → self-devouring → "his hand is stretched out still" (×5) → Assyria as rod, with a heart of its own.

What sets a person's anger off: demand → anger → "Am I in the place of God" (Gen 30:1–2); no regard → very angry → face fell (Gen 4:5); saw no homage → filled with fury → sought to destroy all the Jews (Est 3:5–6); "I thought" → rage (2Ki 5:11–12); afraid → withdraw → enraged (Dan 11:30); heard → filled with wrath → drove him out (Luk 4:28–29); passions at war within → quarrels (Jam 4:1).

Face 3Y. Vexation and grief borne within: Hits / verses: 11 / 11; Who, and at whom: Hannah, David, Job, the Preacher, the helpless; Example verses: 1Sa 1:16; Psa 6:7; Psa 31:9; Job 17:7; Ecc 2:23; Psa 10:14.

One root, two directions (new): what people do to God (provoke) and what one person does to another (Hannah's rival); what a person carries (vexation, grief, sorrow); what God will increase toward Job: Verses: Deu 4:25; 1Sa 1:6, 16; Job 10:17 (AG-119, 141, 116).

Where it sits in the person (new for these words): the face (fell); the eye, soul, body, members; the heart at night; the spirit (quick): Verses: Gen 4:5; Psa 31:9; Job 17:7; Ecc 2:23; Ecc 7:9 (AG-131, 143, 145).

no regard → very angry → face fell (Gen 4:5); ascribed ten thousands → very angry → eyed David (1Sa 18:8–9); walls going forward → very angry → plotted (Neh 4:7–8); sees the honour → angry → gnashes, melts away (Psa 112:9–10).

F.4: What emerged: The instrument has its own heart, and is charged. Isa 10:7; Isa 47:6–7; Zec 1:15; 2Ch 28:9–10 (AG-166, 167).; What it changes elsewhere: Ch 11 and 10.9 hold two of these. The instrument as a party with an inner being of its own is NS for 10.13 (ruling 6.2).; Where: 10.13; 10.9.
sent against a godless nation → but it is in his heart to destroy (Isa 10:6–7).

thought he would come out → angry → went away → servants' question → dipped → flesh restored (2Ki 5:11–14); angry with the priests → leprosy broke out (2Ch 26:19); Naboth's word → vexed and sullen → lay down, turned away his face, ate no food (1Ki 21:4).
his spirit provoked as he saw idols → so he reasoned (Act 17:16–17); many days → greatly annoyed → commanded the spirit → it came out (16:18).

Gen 4:5-6: "Cain was very angry, and his face fell ... Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?"; God reads the anger off the face; what follows in 4:7 is an inner struggle stated as an image: "sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it".

2Ki 5:11-14: Naaman "was angry and went away ... turned and went away in a rage"; his inner thought is quoted ("Behold, I thought that he would surely come out"); the servants talk him round (5:13), and "his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child" (5:14): rage, persuasion, obedience, restoration, with no seat word anywhere.

The strife words are mostly in vice lists and church-order texts, where the inner place is given by the frame: 1Cor 3:3, "you are still of the flesh"; 1Ti 6:4-5, "puffed up with conceit ... depraved in mind" (nous is excluded from M47 by ruling 4, so these do not count as seated); Gal 5:26 ("provoking one another, envying one another") sits between 5:24-25 (flesh crucified, walk by the Spirit) and 6:1.

Eze 20:33, "As I live, declares the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you", answers a thought, "What is in your mind shall never happen ... 'Let us be like the nations ... and worship wood and stone'" (20:32); the wrath poured out goes with bringing out and gathering (20:34), with judgment "face to face" (20:35), and with bringing them "into the bond of the covenant" (20:37): God answers a thought in the mind with an oath by his own life and with his rule.

Outside the verse: Num 11:12 "Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child". The bearer's own, relational and bodily. Moses's displeasure (11:10) comes out as a protest about the bosom he is asked to carry the people in (E v2 data note). Num 11:13 "meat" is spurious.

Where it comes from. From knowing the distance and asking anyway. Abraham says twice, "I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27; 18:31). Gideon has already had his sign (Judg 6:38). The asker knows that the request presses on God's patience.
enemies who "injure my cause … have waited for my life" (Psa 56:5–6).

What it does: "Cain was very angry, and his face fell" (Gen 4:5); Ahab went home "vexed and sullen … lay down on his bed and turned away his face and would eat no food" (1Ki 21:4); In 1Ki 20:43 the same pair, "vexed and sullen", takes him home to Samaria; The movement is inward and downward: face, bed, refusing food.

Where it comes from. From a denial the person cannot reverse: no regard from God for Cain's offering while Abel's is regarded (Gen 4:4–5); the prophet's verdict, "your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people" (1Ki 20:42); Naboth's refusal, "I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers" (1Ki 21:3–4).

(b) Thwarted and made a fool of: Balaam: "Balaam's anger was kindled, and he struck the donkey with his staff" (Num 22:27). When the donkey speaks, he gives his reason: "Because you have made a fool of me. I wish I had a sword in my hand, for then I would kill you" (22:29). The anger is about being shamed, and it wishes to kill; Balak: "Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, and he struck his hands together … 'I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them these three times'" (Num 24:10). It ends in dismissal and the withholding of honour: "the Lord has held you back from honor" (24:11); Naaman: "Naaman was angry and went away, saying, 'Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me …'" (2Ki 5:11), and "he turned and went away in a rage" (5:12). What the anger releases is a disappointed expectation of honour, quoted as his own thought. Pilot §1.4 read the whole movement: rage → persuasion → obedience → restoration; The Ephraimite army, discharged, "became very angry with Judah and returned home in fierce anger" (2Ch 25:10), and later "raided the cities of Judah" (25:13). Anger at being sent away returns as violence against those who sent it.

How it co-exists: With enforced silence first. "Elihu had waited to speak to Job because they were older than he" (32:4), and "I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion" (32:6). Fear and deference hold the anger in, until the others fall silent; Elihu describes the pressure in bodily terms: "I am full of words; the spirit within me constrains me. Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like new wineskins ready to burst. I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:18–20). The held anger is felt as pressure in the belly, and speech is its release.

Part 2 verses: what they add. The one wronged is now God, or God's law, rather than a sister, a friend or the poor: The indignation seizes its bearer: "Hot indignation seizes me because of the wicked, who forsake your law" (Psa 119:53). The bearer is its object as well as its subject. It is framed between comfort in God's rules (119:52) and "Your statutes have been my songs" (119:54). The indignation sits inside a life held by the law it defends; The spirit provoked by what it sees: "while Paul was waiting … his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue … and in the marketplace every day" (Act 17:16–17). This is the same movement as Neh 5:6–7: indignation, then an inner act, then public speech. Here the seat is named in the indignation verse itself; Annoyance that finally acts: the slave girl "kept doing this for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you … come out of her'" (Act 16:18); What annoys him is a true proclamation ("These men are servants of the Most High God", 16:17) from a wrong source; The anger builds over "many days" before the act; The act sets off anger in others: "when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas" (16:19).

How it co-exists: With the sufferer's own speech that explains it. Hannah: "I am a woman troubled in spirit … I have been pouring out my soul before the Lord … I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation" (1Sa 1:15–16). Job: "therefore my words have been rash" (Job 6:3). The vexation is given as the reason the sufferer's speech looks the way it does: drunk to Eli, rash to the friends; With misreading by the onlooker: Eli takes Hannah "to be a drunken woman" (1:13–14).

How it co-exists. With fear, straight after: "David was afraid of the Lord that day, and he said, 'How can the ark of the Lord come to me?'" (2Sa 6:9; 1Ch 13:12). Anger at God and fear of God follow one another in consecutive verses. A new pairing, not read in the batches: With complaint to God: Moses, "Why have you dealt ill with your servant? … Did I conceive all this people? … 'Carry them in your bosom'" (Num 11:11–12); With all-night crying: Samuel (1Sa 15:11). Later, Samuel "grieved over Saul" (15:35). Anger turns to crying out, and then to grief.

Seat: In the verse: none; Outside the verse: Num 11:12 "Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child". The bearer's own, relational and bodily. Moses's displeasure (11:10) comes out as a protest about the bosom he is asked to carry the people in (E v2 data note). Num 11:13 "meat" is spurious; The unit-2 side of these four verses is God's own anger (Num 11:10; 2Sa 6:7; 1Ch 13:10), for unit 2.

Part 2 verses: what they add: The body's end of rivalrous anger: "The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!" (Psa 112:10). What he sees is the righteous man, whose "horn is exalted in honor" (112:9). Seeing the rival's rise ends in the angry one dissolving, not in the spear of 1Sa 18; Contrast seat: "His heart is steady; he will not be afraid" (112:8), said of the righteous one, two verses before. The seat is again named in the one the anger is aimed at (see Neh 4:6 above). Genuine; Rivalry among the disciples: "when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers" (Mat 20:24 = Mar 10:41). What they heard was Jesus's answer about the two brothers' place: "to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant" (Mat 20:23; Mar 10:40); Jesus answers by redefining greatness: "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them … It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant" (Mat 20:25–26; Mar 10:42–43); The anger at a rival's rise is not rebuked directly. The standing it is about is re-defined, so the rise it resented no longer counts. This is a reframing, the §9 and §6 move used on rivalry; Seat : none in-verse.

Where it comes from. Every verse, or the one next to it, names a source, and the sources are inner: Passions at war within: "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel" (Jam 4:1–2). The outer fight is the inner war carried outward; The flesh: "for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?" (1Cor 3:3), after "I could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh" (3:1); Conceit: "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26). "He is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy" (1Ti 6:4); Appetite: the dividers "do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites [belly]" (Rom 16:18); Envy and selfish ambition behind a good act: "Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will … The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me" (Phili 1:15–17). The same outward act, preaching, has opposite inner sources; A depraved mind: "constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1Ti 6:5); Controversies themselves: "foolish, ignorant controversies … breed quarrels" (2Ti 2:23); "avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law" (Tit 3:9).
Gen 4:4–8: Sequence the text gives: regard withheld → anger → face fallen → God reads the face and asks → sin at the door, "rule over it" → killing.

1Sa 1:6–18: Sequence the text gives: provoked year by year → weeping, not eating → heart named by husband → "deeply distressed" (Hebrew bitter of soul) → heart-prayer, lips only → misread as drunk → self-explanation ("vexation") → blessing → eats, face no longer sad.
2Sa 13:20–39: Sequence the text gives: "do not take this to heart" → the king very angry, no act → the brother's hatred waits two years → killing → the king's spirit longs for the killer.

What it does: Abraham: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there" (Gen 18:30), and at the last: "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten" (18:32); Gideon, after the fleece was wet: "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece" (Judg 6:39); The same form appears in two different kinds of asking. Abraham asks for a city he does not belong to. Gideon asks for assurance for himself.

How it co-exists. The test is passed by putting God above kin: Levi "said of his father and mother, 'I regard them not'; he disowned his brothers and ignored his children. For they observed your word" (33:9). Contrast U1 §2 (KS), where kinship grounds the refusal of strife.

Part B: Psa 56:7; 59:13; 69:24; 79:6; Jer 10:25; 18:23; Lam 3:66 (seven verses). The imprecation is a recurring form in part B, as part A's pointer expected: The grounds given:; enemies who "injure my cause … have waited for my life" (Psa 56:5–6); "the sin of their mouths … the cursing and lies" (59:12); "they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded" (69:26): they add to God's striking; "the nations that do not know you … have devoured Jacob" (79:6–7; Jer 10:25 in the same words); Restraint inside the imprecation: "Kill them not, lest my people forget … consume them in wrath … that they may know that God rules over Jacob" (Psa 59:11, 13). See §45; Lam 3:66 comes with "You will give them dullness of heart" (3:65); Seat ; In the verse: none; Outside: Lam 3:65 "dullness of heart". The enemies'. Genuine. Psa 56:6 "my life" (nephesh). Life-sense.

Where it comes from: the agent's own heart: Assyria: "But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few; for he says: 'Are not my commanders all kings?'" (Isa 10:7–8); Babylon: "I was angry with my people … I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. You said, 'I shall be mistress forever,' so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end" (47:6–7). And "who say in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me'" (47:8).

Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Isa 10:7 "heart" ×2; Isa 10:12; Isa 47:8; Isa 47:7 "did not lay these things to heart" was not found in the batches: new as a context seat. Babylon's heart, like Israel's in §36, does not take in what it is doing.

What it does: "What is in your mind shall never happen — the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.' As I live … surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you" (Eze 20:32–33); "I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you … with wrath poured out. And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face" (20:34–35); "Where now is your king, to save you …? Where are all your rulers — those of whom you said, 'Give me a king and princes'? I gave you a king in my anger, and I took him away in my wrath" (Hos 13:10–11).
Where it comes from: The wish in the mind (Eze 20:32); The request for a king (Hos 13:10); Refusal to be inquired of: "I will not be inquired of by you" (Eze 20:31).
Seat. None in-verse. Outside: Eze 20:32 "What is in your mind" (ruach). The people's. Genuine.

Where it comes from: Knowledge suppressed: "what can be known about God is plain to them … So they are without excuse" (Rom 1:19–20); Kindness presumed on: "do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?" (2:4); Judging others while doing the same: "you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself" (2:3).

(v2) Isa 9:8–10:7: Sequence the text gives: pride in rebuilding → struck → "did not turn" → leaders mislead → self-devouring → "his hand is stretched out still" (×5) → Assyria as rod, with a heart of its own; Phenomena: ST · UA.
(v2) Isa 10:5 (UA): Context seat: Isa 10:7 "his heart does not so think … in his heart to destroy"; Whose · check: Assyria's · genuine; Already read in: F v4 §12.1; C v3 §2.1; §: §37.
(v3) Eze 20:33 (KG): Context seat: Eze 20:32 "What is in your mind"; Whose · check: the people's · genuine; Already read in: E v2 §4.1; §: §51.

"For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened" (1:21). They "exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images" (1:23). Then three times "God gave them up" (1:24, 26, 28), each after an exchange (1:23, 25, and "did not see fit to acknowledge God", 1:28).

The original (§4.6a). The English sets "honor" (1:21) against "dishonoring" and "dishonorable" (1:24, 26). The Greek does not: "honor" in 1:21 is doxazō "glorify". "Dishonoring" (1:24) is atimazō and "dishonorable passions" (1:26) is pathē atimias, literally "passions of dishonor". Atimia is the negative of timē "honour" (M71). "Shameless acts" (1:27) is aschēmosynē, "indecency", whose range runs to "nakedness, shame" (Rev 16:15).

It has no room for God: "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psa 10:4); "his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4). Then: "an arrogant man who is never at rest. His greed is as wide as Sheol" (2:5). The swollen soul is set against faith, and joined to restlessness and greed.

Psalm 119 gives one person's whole experience of the insolent: "The insolent utterly deride me, but I do not turn away from your law" (119:51); "The insolent smear me with lies, but with my whole heart I keep your precepts; their heart is unfeeling like fat" (119:69–70); "they have wronged me with falsehood; as for me, I will meditate on your precepts" (119:78); "The insolent have dug pitfalls for me; they do not live according to your law" (119:85); "let not the insolent oppress me" (119:122); The insolent wander from the commandments (119:21). Against them each time, the speaker holds the law, meditates, and asks for a pledge.

The Greek picture is swelling, physioō, "to inflate". In Paul it is set again and again against love: Knowledge. "This 'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1Co 8:1–3). Swelling knowledge is answered not by more knowledge but by being known by God; Love is not. "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant" (1Co 13:4). Before this: "if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge ... but have not love, I am nothing" (13:2); Party; "that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:6–7); Here Paul states what the Hebrew verses showed in story: pride holds what was received "as if you did not receive it"; Talk without power. "Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you ... I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power" (1Co 4:18–20). The arrogance rests on Paul being absent; Where grief belongs. "And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?" (1Co 5:2). Pride stands where mourning should be; Without reason. "puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head" (Col 2:18–19, carried from M09); The new convert. "He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6). The verse joins conceit to the devil's condemnation. It does not say what the devil's condemnation was. I read: it is held for 13.3 (other spirits). It is not built on here; Controversy. "he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension" (1Ti 6:4). Conceit is joined to understanding nothing, and to quarrels; With pleasure. "swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power" (2Ti 3:4–5); Among the others; "quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder" (2Co 12:20); "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26), after "let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (5:25); Conceit is named among the things that set people against each other.

The measure assigned. "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3). The right measure of oneself is what God assigned. It opens with "by the grace given to me".
Lofty opinions. "every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ" (2Co 10:5). Height here is a thought raised against knowing God.

From within. "from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts ... coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person" (Mar 7:21–23). Jesus places pride in the heart.

Scattered in their thoughts. "He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate" (Luk 1:51–52). The pride is located "in the thoughts of their hearts", and that is where it is scattered.

The given-or-taken line is stated outright. "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7): This is the plainest statement in the three batches of what the researcher suspected. Human pride holds as its own what was received; The researcher's word "assumed" fits: the standing is taken up as if it were not given; The right measure is the one God assigns. "not to think of himself more highly than he ought ... according to the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3). I read: where God has height by nature, a person has a measure by gift. Pride is thinking past the gift; Taking God's seat; "takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" (2Th 2:4); Together with Eze 28:2 and Isa 14:13 (batches 1–2), the verses show pride at its full height as a claim to God's own place; I read: God's "Most High" is the place pride reaches for. Batches 1–3 show no one holding it but God; Christ's firstness is grounded, and pleased; "that in everything he might be preeminent. For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell" (Col 1:18–19); His first place rests on what he is: before all things, the one through whom all were made, firstborn from the dead. It is not claimed against anyone; Batch 1 also has Christ's majesty as "received ... from God the Father" (2Pe 1:17), and his seat taken "after making purification for sins" (Heb 1:3); I read: in the verses the Son's height comes with his descent: firstborn from the dead, seated after purification. This bears on 13.1 Lowering himself; God's knowing is what pride meets. "God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God" (Luk 16:15). "he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts" (Luk 1:51). As in batch 2 (1Sa 2:3), God's knowledge is joined to his answer to pride; Other beings in these verses (held, not read in); A messenger of Satan is given against conceit (2Co 12:7); The conceited may fall "into the condemnation of the devil" (1Ti 3:6); Angels greater in might do not blaspheme where the willful do (2Pe 2:11); These are for 13.2 and 13.3. The verses do not say that the devil fell by pride. That is not stated here and is not built on.

Not by comparing. "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor" (Gal 6:3–4). Thinking oneself something when one is nothing is named self-deception.

The boast is not removed. It is moved: The command. "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31; 2Co 10:17). This follows Christ "who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1:30). It is joined to "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends" (2Co 10:18); What to boast in; "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24); The boast is in knowing God, and what is known is his character; The soul's boast. "My soul makes its boast in the Lord; let the humble hear and be glad" (Psa 34:2, carried); Not in my bow. "For not in my bow do I trust ... In God we have boasted continually" (Psa 44:6–8). The psalm then turns: "But you have rejected us" (44:9). The boast in God is kept in the psalm even while the defeat is brought before him; His name. "Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice!" (Psa 105:3; 1Ch 16:10); The worm. "Fear not, you worm Jacob ... you shall rejoice in the Lord; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory" (Isa 41:14–16). The one called a worm is the one who glories; Justified and glorying. "Only in the Lord, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength ... In the Lord all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory" (Isa 45:24–25); The nations. If Israel returns and swears in truth, "nations shall bless themselves in him, and in him shall they glory" (Jer 4:2); Exulting; "all who swear by him shall exult" (Psa 63:11); "Let the righteous one rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!" (Psa 64:10); "that I may glory with your inheritance" (Psa 106:5); The cross. "far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world" (Gal 6:14); Christ, not the flesh. "glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh — though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also" (Php 3:3–4). Paul has standing in the flesh, "I have more", and sets it aside; Hope, sufferings, God. ESV renders kauchaomai "rejoice" here:; "we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings" (Rom 5:2–3); "we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation" (5:11); The same word that elsewhere is a proud boast is here joy in hope, in suffering, and in God; Held fast. "if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope" (Heb 3:6); The conscience. "our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God" (2Co 1:12). The boast is a clear conscience, and its ground is named as grace.

Corinthians 10–12 is one long passage in which Paul is forced to boast, and he turns the boast round: As a fool. "accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool" (2Co 11:16–17). He names the boast foolish while he makes it; Weakness. "If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness" (11:30). What follows is being let down a wall in a basket (11:32–33); Visions. "I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations" (12:1). Then "On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses" (12:5); No more than is seen. "if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me" (12:6); I read: this is the opposite of pride's assumed standing. He holds back even a true boast so that his standing in others' eyes is no higher than what is so; Power in weakness. "I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me ... For when I am weak, then I am strong" (12:9–10); Authority given. "if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you" (2Co 10:8). The authority is given, and it is given for others; "this boasting of mine will not be silenced": that he served them without burdening them (2Co 11:9–10).

God is not the subject of a boast in these verses. He is its right object, and his character is what is boasted in. "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight" (Jer 9:24). The proper boast is knowing God as he is: The boast is moved, not removed. The same impulse that boasts in wisdom, might and riches (Jer 9:23) is turned to God (9:24; 1Co 1:31). It becomes joy in hope and in suffering (Rom 5:2–3); I read: set beside batches 1–3, the human "lifting" is not abolished. Where it rests on oneself it is pride. Where it rests on God it is glory in him. This fits Ch 12 claim C-182 (the boast moved to what God does). It is a reconciliation point when that chapter is touched; Gift excludes self-boasting. "it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Eph 2:8–9). "What do you have that you did not receive?" (1Co 4:7). "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Gal 6:3); This is the researcher's "assumed" in the verses' words: a standing held as one's own when it was received, or thought when it is not so; The contrast with God, from batches 1–3, is that his standing is neither received nor assumed; The measure is assigned. "the area of influence God assigned to us" (2Co 10:13), and in batch 3 "the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3). I read: where God's height is his by nature, a person's rightful standing is a measure given, and pride boasts "beyond limits"; Christ's power in weakness. "my power is made perfect in weakness ... so that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2Co 12:9). The boast in weakness makes room for another's power. This bears on 13.1 Lowering himself, as in batch 3 §3.4; God's steadfast love answers the boast of evil. "Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day" (Psa 52:1). God's character is set over the mighty man's boast, as his mercy answered presumption in batch 2 §3.7.

Proverbs paints the scoffer by what he will not receive: Rebuke; "A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke" (Pro 13:1); "A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise" (15:12). The verse before is "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of man!" (15:11); Hatred of correction. "Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse ... Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you" (Pro 9:7–8). The same rebuke brings out hate in one and love in the other; Wisdom in vain. "A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding" (Pro 14:6). He seeks, and does not find; Learning by his fall; "Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence" (19:25); "When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise" (21:11); The scoffer is not the one who learns. Others learn from what happens to him; Strife. "Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease" (Pro 22:10). "the scoffer is an abomination to mankind" (24:9); Justice and the guilt offering; "A worthless witness mocks at justice" (19:28). "Condemnation is ready for scoffers" (19:29); "Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance" (14:9). They mock the very means of putting guilt right; Delight, and the offer. "How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing ... If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you" (Pro 1:22–23). Scoffing is a delight held on to, and the offer still stands to the one who turns; Alone. "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it" (Pro 9:12); The seat. "Blessed is the man who ... nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psa 1:1–2). The scoffer's seat is set against delight in the law; The warning; "do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong", then "Give ear, and hear my voice" (Isa 28:22–23). Again the opposite of scoffing is hearing; "the scoffer cease ... who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate" (Isa 29:20–21). The scoffer works against the one who reproves. In the same passage "The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the Lord" (29:19); Wine and company; "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise" (Pro 20:1); "the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers", and "none of them calls upon me" (Hos 7:5, 7); In Job's debates; Zophar: "when you mock, shall no one shame you?" (Job 11:3); Job: "after I have spoken, mock on" (21:3); Elihu: "Beware lest wrath entice you into scoffing" (36:18); I read: the charge of scoffing is thrown between the speakers. As with Eliab in batch 2, the verses do not settle that it is true of Job; "Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor" (Pro 3:34, carried). This is the source of Jam 4:6 and 1Pe 5:5.

The mocker mocked. Of Sennacherib, who mocked the Lord: "She despises you, she scorns you — the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you" (2Ki 19:21; Isa 37:22). Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal: "Cry aloud, for he is a god ... perhaps he is asleep", and "there was no voice. No one answered" (1Ki 18:27, 29): I read: mocking here exposes a false claim, of a king who rose against the Holy One, and of a god who does not answer.

A pride word is used of God here. lāʿag "mock" and lîṣ "scorn" are said of God: "the Lord holds them in derision" (Psa 2:4); "you hold all the nations in derision" (Psa 59:8); "Toward the scorners he is scornful" (Pro 3:34); wisdom: "I will mock when terror strikes you" (Pro 1:26); The verses show how God's derision differs from human mocking; Where it comes from. It comes from the one who "sits in the heavens" (Psa 2:4), from the height that batches 1–3 found is his by nature; What it answers. It always answers a rising against him: kings set "against the Lord and against his Anointed" (Psa 2:2), those of whom it says "'Who,' they think, 'will hear us?'" (Psa 59:7), the scorners (Pro 3:34), those who "refused to listen" (Pro 1:24); Whom it never targets. In these verses it is never aimed at the weak, the poor or the sufferer. Human mocking is aimed at exactly those: the poor (Pro 17:5), a father (Pro 30:17), the sufferer (Psa 22:7), builders called "feeble" (Neh 4:2); I read: God's derision is the laughter of the undisputed height at a dispute that cannot succeed. Human mockery is a self-made height looking down on someone made low; God is not mocked. "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7). The mocking of his messengers goes on "until there was no remedy" (2Ch 36:16). This is the batch 1 point again: God's standing is challenged, and is not overturned; The Son is mocked, and does not answer in kind; The one with the undisputed standing is mocked on that very standing: "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Mat 27:29); "He saved others; he cannot save himself" (Mar 15:31); He "made no answer" (Luk 23:9), and he prays "Father, forgive them" (Luk 23:34); I read: in the Son, the majesty of batch 1 does not defend itself against mockery. This is the clearest instance of 13.1 Lowering himself in these words. It joins the batch 1 point that his majesty and his being "delivered into the hands of men" stand side by side (Luk 9:43–44); Mocking exposes a false height. Zion scorns Sennacherib (2Ki 19:21). Elijah mocks a god who does not answer (1Ki 18:27). Here the mocking does not come from pride. It names a claim that is empty.

Pride sense (42). These include: the heart proud or haughty: 2Ch 32:25–26; 2Ch 26:16; Eze 28:2, 5, 17; Eze 31:10; Pro 16:5; Pro 18:12; Psa 101:5; a haughty spirit: Pro 16:18; Ecc 7:8; haughty eyes and looks: Isa 5:15; 2Ki 19:22 and Isa 37:23 (lifting the eyes against the Holy One); the lofty brought low: Isa 10:33; Isa 26:5; Eze 31:14; "do not become proud, but fear": Rom 11:20; Rom 12:16, 2Co 10:5 ("every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God") and Luk 16:15; Obd 3–4 and Jer 49:16 (the nest set high); Isa 3:16 (the daughters of Zion) and Isa 22:16 (Shebna's tomb on the height). These two have no other M-code.

God's height is his own, shown in acts, and not overturned: "robed in majesty ... you are from everlasting" (Psa 93:1–2). "In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries" (Exo 15:7); Majesty goes with what only God does: abasing every proud one and saving by his own hand (Job 40:10–14); "God is not mocked" (Gal 6:7); Human pride, in the verses' own words, is a standing taken or assumed; "you make your heart like the heart of a god" (Eze 28:2); "takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God" (2Th 2:4); "By the strength of my hand I have done it" (Isa 10:13); "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (Gal 6:3); Mostly, pride holds as its own what was given; "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1Co 4:7); In story: Uzziah's strength, Hezekiah's healing, Nebuchadnezzar's God-given majesty, the cherub's beauty, the cedar's height (2Ch 26:15–16; 32:24–25; Dan 5:18–20; Eze 28:17; 31:9–10); This matches the researcher's "mostly assumed": the standing is real, but it is taken up as if it were not received.
Turns toward help (Deu 33:26): Human pride: Turns away from God: "does not seek him" (Psa 10:4).

The boast is moved, not removed: "let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (Jer 9:24); "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" (1Co 1:31); The same word becomes joy in hope and in suffering (Rom 5:2–3, 11); Boasting in weakness: "so that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2Co 12:9); Boasting of others (2Co 7:4; 1Th 2:19); The boast within the measure God assigned (2Co 10:13), as thinking of oneself is within "the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Rom 12:3).

God brings it down: "God opposes the proud" (Jam 4:6); "he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts" (Luk 1:51); "The haughty looks of man shall be brought low ... and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day" (Isa 2:11); "it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psa 75:7); Death too: "Your pomp is brought down to Sheol" (Isa 14:11).

In meeting someone who is wrong or opposed: "restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted" (Gal 6:1). The verse joins the gentle restoring to watching oneself. Two verses on: "if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself" (6:3); "correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance" (2Ti 2:25). The correcting is gentle, and the outcome is left to God; "make a defense … yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1Pe 3:15); "Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?" (1Cor 4:21). Said to those who "are arrogant" (4:18); "to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people. For we ourselves were once foolish" (Tit 3:2–3). The ground of the gentleness is the memory of what "we ourselves" were.

"No other M-code" is a fact about the single verse, not about what it says. In almost every case the inner act sits in the verses next to it. Examples: the proud in Jam 4:6, partiality and "evil thoughts" in Jam 2:4, "very sad" in Luk 18:23, "received him joyfully" in Luk 19:6, and "indignantly" in Mar 14:4. Read in their passages, the 27 fall into six groups.

Jam 2:3 ("You stand over there"): The act: partiality. A gold ring and fine clothing are seated, shabby clothing is sent to stand (2:2–3); What James calls it: "have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?" (2:4); Against it: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (2:5), and "you have dishonored the poor man" (2:6); The poor man is the party acted on. The inner act, judging with evil thoughts, is in those who seat him; 2:4–6 are cited in 10.7, 10.10, Ch 11 and 13.1. 2:3 is not.

3. Needy as an expression to get sympathy or help: What these 27 verses show: Not in these 27, from the poor themselves. No poor person here speaks. Lazarus "desired to be fed" but says nothing. What appears is another face: others speak of the poor, and in John the words of care are a pretext (Joh 12:6). Whether "needy" said by the needy is aimed at help is a matter for the "I am poor and needy" Psalms (Psa 86:1, 70:5, 40:17, 109:22) and Pro 18:23 "The poor use entreaties"..

The `self` pattern catches more than it should. Only five of its ten hits are a speaker calling himself poor: 1Sa 18:23, Psa 40:17, Psa 70:5, Psa 86:1 and Psa 109:22. The other five are Luk 4:18, Isa 61:1, Luk 19:8, Job 29:16 and Job 30:25. The markers are a working aid only: they point to verses to read and decide nothing.

Poor or needy said by the speaker as the ground of a plea: "answer me, for I am poor and needy" (Psa 86:1); "I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God!" (Psa 70:5); "As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psa 40:17).
The poor appealing to others: "The poor use entreaties, but the rich answer roughly" (Pro 18:23); "you hear the desire of the afflicted" (Psa 10:17); "he cry to the Lord against you" (Deu 15:9).

Note for reading. In Psa 40:17, 70:5, 86:1 and 109:22, "poor" in "poor and needy" is H6041 ʿānî, which is tagged M24, and "needy" is H0034 (M09). This was checked in `verse_lexical`. These verses therefore sit on both sides of the M09 / M24 line.

G4202 (porneia, 22 verses, the broadest term) ranges from literal cases (1 Cor 5's incest case, the vice-list entries in Mark 7:21 and Gal 5:19) to a sustained, book-length personification.

Cruelty is defined by the absence of mercy, stated explicitly, not implied. Three of H0394's six verses use the near-identical formula cruel and have no mercy (Jer 6:23, 50:42) or merciless (Jer 30:14); Prov 12:10 makes the same point as a paradox, the mercy of the wicked is cruel, that is, even their gentlest disposition still qualifies as cruelty. Cruelty here is not a separate vice alongside mercilessness; the texts treat the two as the same fact stated twice.
