1.7 God's Spirit as the source of knowledge [D]: "the Spirit of wisdom and understanding … of knowledge and the fear of the Lord" (Isa 11:2); "filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship" (Exo 31:3; 35:31); "through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom … of knowledge" (1Co 12:8); "the Spirit searches everything … the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit … they are spiritually discerned" (1Co 2:10–14); "the Holy Spirit will teach you" (Luk 12:12; Joh 14:26); "we do not know what to pray for … but the Spirit himself intercedes" (Rom 8:26); "he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit" (Rom 8:27)

1.8 Flesh as a way of knowing: "we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh" (2Co 5:16); "set their minds on the things of the flesh … the Spirit" (Rom 8:5) [D3]; "the desires of the flesh and the mind" (Eph 2:3); "his sensuous mind [mind of flesh]" (Col 2:18); "I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh …" (Rom 7:25)

1.9 Conscience and knowledge: "not all possess this knowledge … their conscience, being weak, is defiled" (1Co 8:7, 10) — knowledge shapes the conscience.; "both their minds and their consciences are defiled" (Tit 1:15).; "their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them" (Rom 2:15).

1.10 Heart and mind (nous / dianoia) side by side: "put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts" / "on their hearts … on their minds" (Heb 8:10 / 10:16); "guard your hearts and your minds" (Phili 4:7); The love command lists heart, soul, mind and strength as separate items (Mar 12:30; Mat 22:37; Luk 10:27); Revisit 2026-09-28 (context Mar 12:28–34, Batch F §2): the scribe repeats the command as "heart … understanding [*synesis*] … strength" (12:33). He replaces soul with a knowing word, and Jesus calls the answer wise (12:34). The faculty list is not fixed; what stays constant is "all".; "evil thoughts [reasonings]" come "out of the heart" (Mat 15:19; Mar 7:21); "the reasoning of their hearts" (Luk 9:47)
Soul pierced, heart revealed: "a sword will pierce through your own soul also, so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed" (Luk 2:35).

1.11 ◆ Breath, wind and thought: "When his breath departs … on that very day his plans perish" (Psa 146:4) — the brief's thought link; "he who … creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought" (Amo 4:13); "windy knowledge" (Job 15:2); "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (Ecc 1:17); "Every man is stupid and without knowledge … there is no breath in them" (Jer 10:14; 51:17)

Revisit 2026-09-28: "uttering from the heart lying words" (Isa 59:13) uses *hāgâ* "mutter". The same verb gives "the heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Pro 15:28) and "their hearts devise violence" (Pro 24:2). The heart is an organ of rehearsal, and its content decides its moral character (Batch F §12.2).

Keeping: "I kept the matter in my heart" (Dan 7:28); "he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered" (Pro 11:13) [H]; "Whoever restrains his words … a cool spirit" (Pro 17:27) [H]; "I told no one what my God had put into my heart" (Neh 2:12)
Dividing and discerning: "the word of God … piercing to the division of soul and of spirit … discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart" (Heb 4:12).
Empty words as wind: "windy words" (Job 16:3); "the words of your mouth be a great wind" (Job 8:2); "the speech of a despairing man is wind" (Job 6:26)

Remembering weighs on the soul: "My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me" (Lam 3:20); "I have forgotten what happiness is" (Lam 3:17); "These things I remember, as I pour out my soul" (Psa 42:4, 6).; Revisit 2026-09-28 (contexts Psa 42:4–7 and Psa 77:2–4, Batch F §9.4): memory works either way. In Psa 42 remembering is the turn ("My soul is cast down … therefore I remember you"). In Psa 77 remembering God deepens the fainting of the spirit. "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not" (Psa 103:2) is one of the self-addresses to the soul, now found in five settings (Batch F §15; Batch G §3.2).

Remembering and the spirit: "When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints" (Psa 77:3); "Let me remember my song … meditate in my heart. Then my spirit made a diligent search" (Psa 77:6) [H].

Questioning in the heart, perceived in the spirit: "some of the scribes … questioning in their hearts … Jesus, perceiving in his spirit" (Mar 2:6–8) [H]; "Why do you question in your hearts?" (Luk 5:22); "all were questioning in their hearts concerning John" (Luk 3:15).
Evil reasonings from the heart: "out of the heart come evil thoughts" (Mat 15:19; Mar 7:21); "why do doubts arise in your hearts?" (Luk 24:38); "does not doubt in his heart" (Mar 11:23).
Flesh as a standard of judging: "You judge according to the flesh" (Joh 8:15); "set their minds on the things of the flesh" (Rom 8:5).

8. ◆ Soul-ish vs spiritual — psychikos / pneumatikos: "The natural [*psychikos*] person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God … they are spiritually discerned" (1Co 2:14) [D1]; "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body … not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual" (1Co 15:44–46); "worldly [*psychikoi*] people, devoid of the Spirit" (Jude 19) [D3]; [lexical; Claude reading] In these verses the adjective formed from *soul* is set against the adjective formed from *spirit*. It is the clearest place in the data where soul and spirit are contrasted as two orders, rather than paralleled (cf. depiction v1 §3.4 on Heb 4:12 and 1Co 15:45).

0. Data notes (short): No pre-filter applies. There is no M42, M61 or M72 in this batch.; Death — v3 note (replaces the v1 note). In v1 and v2 the death words were filed outside the M-codes ("die" in T3, "death" in T10), so §1–§13 read the life side only. After #1880 both also carry M25. The death side is read in §16, and the earlier sections carry Revisit (delta) notes where it bears on them.; Tags that would mislead in the delta: "the heart of the seas" (Eze 28:8) = midst; the "flesh" of an ox (Exo 21:28) and the "meat" pots (Exo 16:3).; Not misleading, but lexically marked (kept, read in §16): *nephesh* = dead body (Lev 21:11; Num 6:6; 19:11, 13, 18); *nephesh* = "willing" (Gen 23:8); the sea's "living things" (Rev 8:9; 16:3); "heart" as the ESV surface for *nephesh* (Pro 19:18; 1Sa 2:33).; Tags that would mislead a reading (noted, and not read as the cluster's sense): "alive / living" (M25); = "raw" flesh (Lev 13:10–24; 1Sa 2:15); = "fresh [living] water" (Lev 15:13); = "wild beasts" (Psa 79:2; Hos 13:8; Eze 39:17; Lev 5:2); Generic verbs in M23: "multiply" (H7235), "be able / can" (H3201); "meet / toward / against" (H7122) in M37: ordinary encounter, not foreknowledge; M71 surfaces used in other senses: "greatness" = arrogance of heart (Isa 9:9; 10:12); "descendants" (1Sa 2:33); "proceeds" (Act 5:3); "color" (Dan 7:28); "bring / lead" (G5342, M70): Mar 9:17, 20; Act 5:16; "heart" = "midst": "the heart of the seas" (Eze 27:27); "in the heart of the oak" (2Sa 18:14)

The formula: "as the Lord lives and as your soul lives" (1Sa 20:3; 25:26; 2Sa 11:11); "as the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2Ki 2:2, 4, 6; 4:30); "As your soul lives, O king, I do not know" (1Sa 17:55); "As you live, my lord" (1Sa 1:26; 2Sa 14:19); "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity" (1Ki 1:29; 2Sa 4:9); "As the Lord lives, who made our souls" (Jer 38:16); "As God lives, … who has made my soul bitter" (Job 27:2); [lexical; Claude reading] The oath sets the other person's *nephesh* beside the Lord's own life as the thing that guarantees the word. To swear by someone's soul is to stake one's word on their life. In the second form, the Lord is identified by what he has done to the soul: redeemed it, made it, made it bitter.

What the sequences show [Claude reading]: The oath marks adherence at a cost.; Elisha's triple oath is the price of the double spirit.; The Shunammite uses Elisha's own oath against him. Her bitterness of soul becomes a hold on the prophet that he cannot refuse.; Uriah's oath by David's soul is kept against David's wish. The wine that should have lowered his guard fails (a failed threshold — Batch F §7). He dies for keeping it.; The oath by the soul can guard a life while refusing a life. Zedekiah swears secretly by "who made our souls" to spare Jeremiah's life. He then declines the life offered to him (38:17, 20), from fear (38:19). The oath and the refusal are in one conversation.; 1Sa 17:55 stands on the threshold of 18:1. A formal oath by Saul's soul immediately precedes the knitting of Jonathan's soul to David's.; The oath misused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (Gehazi, 2Ki 5:20; §13.2).; Revisit (Batch H): God swears by his own soul: "The Lord God has sworn by himself [*his nephesh*]" (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.; The oath answers a claim of vengeance. The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf (Batch H §1.4).; Revisit (delta) — the oath with death in view: The oath formula frames the nearness of death. "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.; A life pledged for a life. Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … deliver our lives from death" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "Our life for yours even to death!" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. They pledge their own *nephesh*.; An oath on a life, broken after a spirit comes (context 1Sa 19:4–12): Jonathan: "he took his life in his hand and struck down the Philistine … Why then will you sin against innocent blood?" (5); "Saul listened … Saul swore, 'As the Lord lives, he shall not be put to death'" (6); War again; David's victory (8); "a harmful spirit from the Lord came upon Saul" (9) [O]
Other texts where the soul turns against its own life: "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 10:1; 9:21)

Opposed to Spirit | "to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace" (Rom 8:6); "if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Rom 8:13); Gal 6:8; Rom 8:12

The Spirit gives life [D1/D2/D3]: "the law of the Spirit of life" (Rom 8:2); "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" (2Co 3:6); "written … with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts" (2Co 3:3); "If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (Gal 5:25); "he … will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit" (Rom 8:11); "although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life" (Rom 8:10) [U]; [Claude reading] Context sets "flesh" as: mortality to be lived in faithfully (Gal 2:20; Phili 1:22); Christ's own path (Heb 10:20); an orientation that ends in death (Rom 8:6, 13); Paul uses all three within a few chapters. In Phili 1:21–24 he weighs "to live in the flesh" against "to depart" for the sake of others.

Persuading the heart (the other M77 verb): "By this we shall … reassure our heart before him" (1Jo 3:19); "if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God" (1Jo 3:21); "put no confidence in the flesh … though I myself have reason for confidence in the flesh also" (Phili 3:3–4) [D1]; "we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience" (2Co 5:11)

12.5 Other: "why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit" (Act 5:3) [D1]; "my heart was glad … my flesh also will dwell in hope" (Act 2:26); "who has … outraged the Spirit of grace" (Heb 10:29) [D1]

The king's heart and a false report of death (context 2Sa 13:28–39): "let not my lord the king so take it to heart as to suppose that all the king's sons are dead, for Amnon alone is dead" (33); Weeping (36); Absalom flees (37–38); "the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead" (39); [Claude reading] The heart is told not to receive a false death. The spirit, over three years, is comforted about a true one. Heart and spirit take the news of death on different timescales. Compare Jacob (§2): the heart numb, the spirit revived.

Qohelet's heart reasons to the shared breath, then leaves the spirit's destination open (Ecc 3:18–21). This is the fullest statement that the breath does not mark man off from beast (§1.1). It is also the place where the difference is left unknown rather than denied.

Flesh bears fruit for death; Spirit is the new way | "while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions … bear fruit for death" (Rom 7:5) → "we serve in the new way of the Spirit" (7:6) [D3]; "the mind on the flesh is death" (Rom 8:6); "live according to the flesh you will die" (8:13); "the law of the Spirit of life has set you free … from the law of sin and death" (8:2) [D1]

The Spirit sets the term of Simeon's life (Luk 2:26). His release is peace (2:29). His next words move to Mary's soul pierced and "thoughts from many hearts" revealed (2:35). One scene holds Spirit, death, soul and heart.

16.11 Before and after: death as the frame of a blessing, an evidence, a burial: "let not my lord take it to heart" (2Sa 13:33; §16.6); "he who stays in this city shall die … he who goes out … shall have his life as a prize of war" (Jer 21:9; 38:2; §5.1)

14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: Life is held in the breath and the soul, and it is God's to give and gather.; "Living soul" is shared with the animals. God's breathing is what marks Gen 2:7.; One decision of God's heart could gather every breath back (Job 34:14–15).; In the flood narrative God's heart changes while man's heart does not (Gen 6:5–6 → 8:21).; *rûaḥ* moves across senses within a single passage, and the passage uses the movement: Eze 37: carrying Spirit → breath → winds → "my Spirit within you"; Judg 15: rushing Spirit → one's own spirit returning; Jon 4: an appointed wind that makes the soul wish to die; Strength and hardness are one word. *ḥāzaq* is courage, hardening and the nerve to kill, according to what the heart is set toward (§3.3). This mirrors the tender heart (Batch F §6): neither softness nor strength of heart has a fixed moral value.; Revisit (Batch H §7.4): more words of this kind — *nāṣar* (keep the heart / the "guarded" wily heart), *šāmar*, vengeance, fatness of soul and of heart, *šāgâ*, kinship-flesh.; The inner components give way in order. Samson (Judg 16): the soul vexed; the heart told; the strength gone; the Lord gone; The strength returns only when asked for, and joined to the soul's consent to die.; Jacob (Gen 45): heart numb → spirit revived by words and sight.; The soul is what one swears by and what one bargains for.; Oaths "as your soul lives" mark adherence at a cost (Elisha, the Shunammite, Uriah) or protection with fear (Zedekiah).; Souls are hunted for bread (Eze 13) and "captured" by the wise (Pro 11:30).; Nothing can be given in return for a soul (Mic 6:7–8; Mat 16:26).; Eating and drinking recur at inner thresholds, now in three registers: the merry heart (Batch F §7); the heart sustained by bread before it is made merry (Judg 19:5, 8); the soul that blesses after a meal and wine (Gen 27:25); Also: the sad heart at a feast that turns to prayer (Hannah, Nehemiah), and the wine-threshold refused (Uriah).; Enticement and stirring show how other agents reach the inner seat: God stirs human spirits (Cyrus, Pul, the remnant).; God sends an other-spirit to entice through prophets' mouths (1Ki 22).; God allures and speaks to the heart (Hos 2:14).; Desire, gods and false teachers entice hearts and souls.

13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Unclean spirits recognise the Son of God (Mar 3:11) and obey him (Mar 1:27).; Spirits either confess Jesus come in the flesh or are "the spirit of the antichrist" (1Jo 4:2–3).; They must be tested (1Jo 4:1), and the spirit of error stands against the Spirit of truth (1Jo 4:6).; The Lord can dispatch a lying spirit (1Ki 22:23). Ministering spirits serve (Heb 1:14).; Flesh in relating to God: "All flesh" is humanity as it comes to God: all flesh comes in prayer (Psa 65:2), sees salvation and glory (Luk 3:6; Isa 40:5), and blesses (Psa 145:21).; Covenant is cut in the flesh, and its inner counterpart is the circumcised heart (§7.2).; Flesh vs spirit as powers: Isa 31:3; Joh 6:63; 1Co 5:5; Jer 17:5.; The "life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11) is the ground of atonement.; God is shown with his own heart and soul in these relations: his soul avenges (Jer 5:9) and he swears by it (Amo 6:8); he acts with all his heart and soul (Jer 32:41); he wishes for a heart in his people (Deu 5:29); his heart recoils in compassion (Hos 11:8); his soul delights in the servant (Isa 42:1); he gives up the beloved of his soul (Jer 12:7); the priest acts according to his heart and soul (1Sa 2:35); Speech and the heart. The heart speaks inwardly ("in the heart", §1.3), is spoken to ("to the heart" = comfort, §1.4), and its speech either matches the mouth or is betrayed by it. Hebrew prayer is an act of the heart that may or may not reach the lips.; Fringe worth keeping: *kāvôd* as the inner self (§3.2) — a possible inner-being term outside M47; the soul asked to die (§2); the double portion of another's spirit (2Ki 2:9); the dying soul naming a child and the returning spirit naming a spring (§1.8); Isaac's soul giving the blessing (§12); Qoheleth testing his own heart (Ecc 2:1); the Gentile's heart-and-conscience law-court (Rom 2:15); the flesh-then-breath sequence of the dry bones (Eze 37:6–8); "gain the whole world and forfeit his soul" (Mat 16:26); "transgression speaks [as an oracle] deep in his heart" (Psa 36:1); the heart with "highways to Zion" (Psa 84:5); "absent in body … present in spirit" (Col 2:5)
Holding it fast: "I hold fast my righteousness … my heart does not reproach me" (Job 27:6); "He still holds fast his integrity" (Job 2:3).
The righteous regard animal life: "Whoever is righteous has regard for the life [*nephesh*] of his beast" (Pro 12:10).

*Ṭāman*, "to hide, bury". A thing is put into or under something. Achan's plunder is "hidden in the earth inside my tent" (Joshua 7:21). Moses "hid him in the sand" (Exodus 2:12). An enemy's net is hidden in the path (Psalm 140:5). It is also the word for the sluggard who "buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it back to his mouth" (Proverbs 19:24).

Hiding from God: In each scene where a person hides from God, something of God is perceived first: a sound (Genesis 3:10), God naming himself (Exodus 3:6), "the terror of the Lord, and … the splendor of his majesty" (Isaiah 2:10), "the face of him who is seated on the throne, and … the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).; Adam hid because he knew he was naked (Genesis 3:10).; Moses "hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God" (Exodus 3:6), and no wrong is named.; At the end, people call "to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us'", for "who can stand?" (Revelation 6:16–17).; Job names the one condition on which he will not hide: "Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me" (Job 13:20–21). In his words, it is the dread that makes a person hide.; None of it works. "Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth?" (Jeremiah 23:24). "There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves" (Job 34:22). Isaiah names what the attempt does: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay" (Isaiah 29:15–16).; That nothing is hidden from God is the same fact for everyone, and it falls very differently.; For the one who suffers it is comfort: "O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you" (Psalm 38:9).; For the one being made it is wonder: "My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret" (Psalm 139:15), and the psalmist answers, "my soul knows it very well" (139:14).; For the one who has done wrong it is judgement: "I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore" (Hosea 5:3).

Hiding from people: Much of the hiding in Scripture is from people who could do harm, and in these verses it is the weaker side that hides. "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). "The poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). When Israel hid in the caves, "all the people followed him trembling" (1 Samuel 13:7).; Often the verse records not the feeling of the one who hides but someone else's counsel to hide.; Jonathan: "Saul my father seeks to kill you … Stay in a secret place and hide yourself" (1 Samuel 19:2).; God to Elijah: "hide yourself by the brook Cherith" (1 Kings 17:3).; Where the feeling is named, it is fear.; Jacob fled from Laban "secretly", and he said why: "Because I was afraid" (Genesis 31:27, 31).; Joseph of Arimathea was "a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews". The same verse ends with him going to Pilate and taking away the body (John 19:38).; Hiding can be good sense: "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it" (Proverbs 22:3). It ends when the news changes. The men who had hidden in the hills "heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle" (1 Samuel 14:22).; And sometimes hiding is refused, or impossible.; The servant chooses not to hide: "I gave my back to those who strike … I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6).; No one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend" (Psalm 55:12–13).

Hiding what I hold: A person can hide what he has done. Achan tells it in order: "when I saw … then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent" (Joshua 7:21). Joshua had to ask him first: "do not hide it from me" (7:19).; What happens next differs.
It fails, and fear follows. Moses "struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand" (Exodus 2:12). When it came out, "Moses was afraid, and thought, 'Surely the thing is known'" (2:14).

The hidden trap: In the Psalms a purpose is hidden in order to catch someone. "They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, 'Who can see them?'" (Psalm 64:5). The next verse says where the purpose was hidden first: "For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (64:6).; The one it is set for prays out of his weakness. "When my spirit faints within me, you know my way! In the path where I walk they have hidden a trap for me" (Psalm 142:3). "No one cares for my soul" (142:4). It is worse when it comes from those he had prayed for: "Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them" (Jeremiah 18:20).; And the trap turns. "In the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught" (Psalm 9:15). The soul the pit was dug for (Psalm 35:7) is the soul that rejoices: "Then my soul will rejoice in the Lord" (35:9). The one taken "out of the net they have hidden for me" says, "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:4–5).
Where the fear stands. It comes before the hiding (Genesis 3:10; Matthew 25:25) or after it fails (Exodus 2:14). Those who hide another are, in one verse, "not afraid" (Hebrews 11:23).

What carries it instead of a seat: the question spoken aloud: "What does this mean?" (Act 2:12); "who is this about whom I hear such things?" (Luk 9:9, context); the gaze: "The disciples looked at one another" (Joh 13:22); a reflexive pronoun: Act 10:17 "inwardly perplexed" is *en heautō*, "in himself". The inner location is there, but through a pronoun, not a seat word.; the body of the other party: in Dan 5:6 the king's "color changed … his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together". The body tells the alarm while his lords are perplexed.

(b) A people hiding under pressure.; Verses: 1Sa 13:6; 14:11, 22; Pro 28:28; Job 24:4; Deu 7:20; Jer 49:10; 2Ki 7:12.; Where it comes from: "when the men of Israel saw that they were in trouble (for the people were hard pressed), the people hid themselves in caves and in holes and in rocks and in tombs and in cisterns" (1Sa 13:6). The next verse gives the inner state: "all the people followed him trembling" (13:7). Also "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Pro 28:28), and "the poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). Hiding is the posture of the weaker party.; What it leads to: the enemy's contempt, "Look, Hebrews are coming out of the holes" (1Sa 14:11). Reversal when news changes: "when all the men … who had hidden themselves … heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them" (1Sa 14:22). Hiding ends when fear is lifted by hearing.; Jer 49:10 is the end of this strand: "he is not able to conceal himself".; 2Ki 7:12 is a suspicion of hiding. The king reads the Syrians' empty camp as an ambush ("they have gone out of the camp to hide themselves"). His fear projects hiding onto the enemy, and he is wrong.

Where it comes from: the attempt to hide. "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?'" (Isa 29:15). The next verse names what that attempt does: "You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay …?" (29:16). Hiding from God inverts creature and creator.

(a) Concealing one's own wrong. Each case has its own sequence: Achan: "when I saw … then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent" (Jos 7:21); Joshua: "tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me" (7:19); Achan: "Truly I have sinned" (7:20); "behold, it was hidden in his tent" (7:22); Seeing, coveting, taking, hiding, being demanded to disclose, confessing, being found.; Moses: "He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand" (Exo 2:12). When the deed surfaces: "Moses was afraid, and thought, 'Surely the thing is known'" (2:14). Concealment fails, and fear follows.; The hidden adultery: "it is hidden from the eyes of her husband" (Num 5:13). The next verse: "the spirit of jealousy comes over him" (5:14). Where a deed is hidden, suspicion grows in the other person.; Job's denial: "if I have concealed my transgressions as others do by hiding my iniquity in my heart [*chob*, bosom], because I stood in great fear of the multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence" (Job 31:33–34). The verse names the motive for concealing sin: fear of social contempt. Job denies he acted on it.; The lepers: they hid the plunder (2Ki 7:8), then "said to one another, 'We are not doing right … If we are silent … punishment will overtake us'" (7:9). Conscience reverses concealment into telling.; Concealment as savouring: "Though evil is sweet in his mouth, though he hides it under his tongue, though he is loath to let it go and holds it in his mouth" (Job 20:12–13). The hidden sin is kept because it is enjoyed.; Not hiding at all: "the look on their faces bears witness against them; they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it" (Isa 3:9). The face discloses: shamelessness.

How it co-exists.; Herod: "Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man … When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly" (Mar 6:20). Fear, knowledge, perplexity and gladness are all present in one man towards one prophet, and the perplexity keeps him listening.; Amazement: "all were amazed and perplexed" (Act 2:12).; The body of another man: Belshazzar's "color changed … his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Dan 5:6) while his lords were perplexed (5:9).; Anguish of love: "I am perplexed about you" (Gal 4:20), after "my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth" (4:19).; A limit held: "perplexed, but not driven to despair" (2Cor 4:8). The perplexity is bounded, and the neighbouring verses set it inside "God … has shone in our hearts" (4:6) and "this treasure in jars of clay" (4:7).

What it leads to. Mostly, something from outside ends it: "While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them" (Luk 24:4); "the men … stood at the gate" and "the Spirit said to him" (Act 10:17, 19); "Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice" (Act 2:14); the queen names Daniel (Dan 5:10–12); Herod "sought to see him" (Luk 9:9); Perplexity ends when an interpreter or a meeting arrives.

Isaiah 1:29 — "the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen": The oracle opens as a lawsuit: *"Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth"* (v2). The charge goes to the inner being: *"Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me"* (v2); *"The ox knows its owner … but Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (v3); *"The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint"* (v5); Their worship goes on, and the Lord refuses it: *"I do not delight in the blood of bulls"* (v11); *"your appointed feasts my soul hates"* (v14); *"even though you make many prayers, I will not listen"* (v15).; Then the choice is laid before them, in the same two-sided shape as Isa 7:15: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"* (v16–17); *"Come now, let us reason together"*, with the offer that sins *"like scarlet"* shall be *"as white as snow"* (v18); the two outcomes: *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (v19–20); Being willing, and refusing (here H3985, a different word from Isa 7), are the two sides of the choice. Eating, and being eaten, are its two outcomes.; The oracle ends with those who did not take the offer. v29–31 is figurative speech, and the figure is the point: *"they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"*; *"you shall be like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water"*; *"the strong shall become tinder, and his work a spark, and both of them shall burn together"*; The things they desired and chose become the picture of what they themselves become. They chose oaks and gardens, and they become a withering oak and a garden with no water. The choice comes back as an image of the chooser. The last line goes further: the strong man’s own *"work"* is the spark that sets him alight. What he made burns him, *"with none to quench them"*.; Shame comes first in the verse: *"ashamed"*, *"blush"* (H0954, H2659). The chooser is ashamed of the very thing that was desired and chosen. What drew the desire becomes the cause of the shame.

Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations": The Lord sees beneath the choosing: *"For I know their works and their thoughts"* (v18).; The tremblers are promised the opposite outcome: *"You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice"* (v14).

Choices weighed by another: The book does not let these evaluations have the last word. Job is the one the Lord calls *"a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil"* (1:8). Of Eliphaz and his friends the Lord says *"you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has"* (42:7); Elihu is not named.; The choice Elihu pressed is made, in his own verb, but only when Job sees the Lord: *"now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent"* (42:5–6).

Where it is placed. The verses place this in the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way"* (Pro 16:9); *"who plan evil things in their heart"* (Psa 140:2); *"the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1Ki 12:33); *"the purposes of the heart"* (1Co 4:5); *"every intention of the thoughts of his heart"* (Gen 6:5)

The planning shows only in small signs.; *"I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jer 11:19). Jeremiah did not see the plan aimed at him.; *"they intended to do me harm"* (Neh 6:2). The sailors of Acts 27 plan under uncertainty. They act *"on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix"* (v12) and *"supposing that they had obtained their purpose"* (v13). 10.7 Choosing and setting direction, new section *Planning* | The account of looking ahead. Planning carries a choice ahead (Gen 11:6; Pro 16:9). It covers: weighing first (Luk 14:28–33; Pro 31:15–16; Judg 19:30); planning without knowing (Act 27:10–14, 39–41; Rom 1:13; Jam 4:15); a plan carrying a person's word (2Co 1:17–18); planning together and parting (Act 15:37–39; Luk 23:51–52); planning for another's good (Dan 6:3–4), with the king's planning measured against God's (2Sa 14:13–14); a purpose held (Psa 17:3, 5; Act 11:23; 2Ti 3:10; 1Ch 29:18; Rom 8:6–7; Isa 26:3); devised from one's own heart (1Ki 12:32–33; Neh 6:8); the plan and its outcome (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38–39; Psa 21:11; Dan 11:24; Gen 50:20); seen and disclosed (1Ch 28:9; 1Co 4:3–5) | New section

A resolve reached after weighing, then turned. *"her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly"* (Mat 1:19). The next verse: *"But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (1:20). The resolve was still being weighed, and God redirected it.

Cleansing, after reasoning: *"Come now, let us reason together … though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow … If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isa 1:18–20). This is the one place in the set where the will is invited with "if". Both ways are set out, as in *Life and death set before a person* (10.7).
Overruled by objection. *"they wished to set me at liberty … But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar"* (Act 28:18–19).

Joseph. *"being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (Mat 1:19–20). He was unwilling to shame her, he resolved, and he went on considering. Then God spoke into the considering.

The return: *"my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High"* (4:34), and *"he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand"* (4:35); *"those who walk in pride he is able to humble"* (4:37).

2.2 Passages where Scripture itself puts them together: Pro 1:29–31. Did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel, are filled with their own devices: choosing, willing and devising in one sentence. Earlier in the same chapter, *"if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood'"* (1:10–11) puts the will's "no" right against a group plot. That is plotting as written in 10.10.; Psa 81:11–12. Would not submit, given over to stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.; Isa 30:1, 9, 15–16. A plan *"but not mine"*; unwilling to hear; unwilling, and *"No! We will flee upon horses."* The refusal and the people's own plan are in their own mouth together.; 1Ch 28:19–21. The plan from the hand of the Lord, and *"every willing man who has skill"*. This is the positive pairing: a plan given, and the willing who carry it out.; Gen 24:5–8. Planning ahead allows for another person's will (*"Perhaps the woman may not be willing"*).; 2Sa 13:24–28. A planner presses another's will until it gives way, and the plan goes on to murder.; Mat 1:19–20. Unwilling, then resolved, while still considering, then redirected by God.; Act 12:3–5. Herod's intending is set beside the church's prayer.; 2Co 1:15–17. Wanting, then plans, then the question of a divided word.; Act 27:42–43. One man's wish against a group's plan.; Dan 4:27–35. Counsel offered and not taken; the human will made absolute; the Most High *"does according to his will"*; reason returned.

Knowing is not enough. Belshazzar *"knew all this"* and did not humble his heart (Dan 5:22). In the plan set, God *"understands every plan"* (1Ch 28:9). The will set adds that the person's own knowing does not move the will.

The chosen are set against others in the passage's own words: those who refused to love the truth and had pleasure in unrighteousness (2Th 2:10–12); those who profess to know God and deny him by works (Tit 1:16); an assembly that judges *"with evil thoughts"* (Jam 2:4); kings of one mind with the beast, and those whose names are not written (Rev 17:8, 13); Stephen's accusers, *"uncircumcised in heart and ears"* (Act 7:51)

1 Kings 8:48 (and 2 Chronicles 6:38): "if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul … and pray to you toward … the city that you have chosen": Solomon dedicates the house. Before the prayer he recalls two choosings: *"I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house … But I chose David to be over my people Israel"* (v16). He also recalls David's heart: *"you did well that it was in your heart"* (v18). David was not allowed to build (v19).; The prayer that follows is a run of cases. In each, someone far from the house prays toward it, and Solomon asks God to hear in heaven. The heart is named throughout: *"each knowing the affliction of his own heart and stretching out his hands toward this house"* (v38); *"render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways (for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind)"* (v39); *"that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land"* (v40); The case of v48 is the hardest one, captivity: *"If they sin against you—for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy"* (v46). Then the inner turning, in steps: *"yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive"* (v47). Literally, "bring it back to their heart" (*šûb*, H7725N, with the heart).; *"and repent and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly'"* (v47); *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies … and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name"* (v48); "Repent" in v47 and v48 is *šûb* (*to return: repent*; H7725O), the same verb as "turn their heart". The turning happens in the enemy's land, far from the city. The whole heart and the whole soul are in it. The prayer is directed toward the chosen city.

The frame the book sets: Before any friend speaks, the book says who Job is, twice: the narrator: *"that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil"* (1:1); the Lord: *"there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil"* (1:8); Job's choosing is already named there, in its refusing side: he *"turned away from evil"*.; At the end the book gives a verdict on the friends: *"the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite"*: *"My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has"* (42:7). The verdict is about how they spoke *of God*. Elihu is not named in it, either way.; So every evaluation of Job's choices in these speeches is made by someone the book does not let have the last word.

Job 15:5 — Eliphaz: "your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty": Eliphaz weighs Job by his words. He opens with *"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge"* (v2), and charges *"you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God"* (v4). Then he names the choice: *"For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty"* (v5). He reads it this way: something inside, iniquity, teaches the mouth; the mouth then chooses a crafty tongue; From that he gives the verdict: *"Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you"* (v6).; He takes his evaluation further inside. He moves from the mouth to the heart, eyes and spirit: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?"* (v12–13). For Eliphaz, the words show what the heart has chosen.; His grounds for judging are age and tradition: *"Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father"* (v10); *"what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers"* (v18); His picture of the outcome is the wicked man's end (v20–35).; Set against the book's frame, his charge *"you are doing away with the fear of God"* (v4) runs against the narrator's and the Lord's *"one who feared God"* (1:1, 8). The Lord's verdict in 42:7 is on how Eliphaz spoke of God, not directly on this charge. Still, the man Eliphaz says has chosen the tongue of the crafty is the one the Lord twice calls *"my servant Job"* (42:7–8).

The Hebrew Bible: The source is the *lēv* (heart), not the brain. Examples are Proverbs 4:23 ("from it flow the springs of life") and Genesis 6:5 ("every intention of the thoughts of his heart").
The New Testament: Mark 7:21 says "from within, out of the heart, come evil thoughts." The heart here is the moral and volitional centre of the person.

Classical theology: Some thoughts are also said to come from outside influences, such as divine prompting or temptation. Paul, for example, speaks of "taking every thought captive" (2 Corinthians 10:5).

Where they seem to agree (Claude's reading, worth testing).: Thought isn't simply self-authored.; Science: most processing is automatic and unconscious. Predictive-processing models describe the brain as constantly generating expectations before we are aware of them.; Philosophy: phenomenology observes that thoughts arrive rather than being made.; Bible: the heart runs deeper than we can see into. Jeremiah 17:9–10 says the heart is beyond knowing except by God, and in Psalm 139:23 the psalmist asks God to "know my thoughts."; Thought is shaped by what it takes in and dwells on.; Science: neuroplasticity. Repeated patterns strengthen connections.; Philosophy: Vygotsky's view that language and culture are internalised.; Bible: Proverbs 4:23 (guard the heart), Romans 12:2 (be transformed by the renewing of the mind) and Philippians 4:8 (think on these things).

1. From within: the heart is where they come from.: Mark 7:21 and Matthew 15:19 say it directly: "from within, out of the heart … come evil thoughts."; Genesis 6:5 speaks of "the intention of the thoughts of his heart," and Luke 1:51 of "the thoughts of their hearts."; Also Hebrews 4:12, Luke 2:35, 1 Chronicles 29:18, Matthew 9:4 and Luke 5:22.; In these verses thoughts are never located in the head. They come out of the heart, the centre of the person.

2. Thoughts arise before they are chosen. Several verses describe thoughts that happen *to* the person: Ezekiel 38:10 has two stages: "thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme." First something rises, then the person works on it. [lexical] The Hebrew there is *dᵉvārîm* (H1697, "words" or "things"), literally "things will come up on your heart."; In Job 20:2, "my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me." The thoughts *respond to* an inner state.; In Daniel 7:28, "my thoughts greatly alarmed me." The thoughts act on the person.; In Romans 2:15, "conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them." They are like inner voices arguing with each other.; So in these verses the person is both where thoughts come from and on the receiving end of them.

4. Knowing a thought is separate from producing it. 1 Corinthians 2:11 says only "the spirit of that person" knows a person's thoughts, and only God's Spirit knows God's. Separately, God searches and knows human thoughts (Psalm 139:23; 1 Chronicles 28:9; Psalm 94:11; 1 Corinthians 3:20), and so does Jesus (Luke 5:22, 6:8, 11:17; Matthew 9:4, 12:25).: *Caveat:* in 1 Corinthians 2:11 the Strong's number is G3588, the Greek article. The word "thoughts" is supplied by the translation; the Greek says "the things of a person."

4.2 What thoughts are: Inner speech. 21 of the rows (H0559, *ʾāmar*, "to say") are places where the Hebrew says "he *said*" and the ESV renders it "he thought," as in 1 Samuel 18:11: "Saul thought, 'I will pin David…'" The Greek *dialogismos* (G1261) and *logismos* (G3053) are also built on *logos*, "word" [lexical]. In these texts, to think is to speak inwardly. *Caveat:* how many rows show this depends on the ESV's choices.; Devising or planning. H4284 *maḥăšāvāh* (from H2803 *ḥāšav*, "to devise"). These thoughts are designs with a direction. They can be just (Proverbs 12:5), evil (Isaiah 59:7), or God's own plan (Micah 4:12). Because they point somewhere, they can be judged, and they can be abandoned (Isaiah 55:7).; Likening, or interpreting. H1819 *dāmāh* ("to resemble") is used in Psalm 50:21: "you thought that I was one like yourself." Many rows record thoughts that were wrong: Genesis 38:15, Mark 6:49, Luke 24:37, Matthew 20:10, Acts 12:9, Judges 3:24 and 2 Kings 5:11. So a thought is a reading of reality, not reality itself.; Something that grows and matures. 1 Corinthians 13:11: "I thought like a child … I gave up childish ways."; Transient, yet weighty. Human thoughts are "but a breath" (Psalm 94:11) and "futile" (1 Corinthians 3:20). Yet God weighs them (Proverbs 15:26), and before the flood they were the measure of human wickedness (Genesis 6:5). God's thoughts, by contrast, are "very deep" (Psalm 92:5), "vast" (Psalm 139:17) and "higher" (Isaiah 55:8–9).
The English word "thought" picks up rows that aren't about the inner life. 1 Timothy 3:7 ("well thought of"), Acts 15:38, 2 Corinthians 9:5 and Philippians 2:25.

5. Suggested exclusions. Idiomatic uses such as "well thought of" (1 Tim 3:7) and "thought it necessary" (2 Cor 9:5, Phil 2:25).

4. One word covers both inner reasoning and outward dispute. *Dialogismos* is rendered "thoughts" (Mark 7:21), but also "quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8), "disputing" (Philippians 2:14) and "opinions" (Romans 14:1). The same activity happens inside a person as an inner conversation and between people as argument.

H7476 *raʿyôn*. Only Daniel 7:28 is in the file. It is expected also in Daniel 2:29, 2:30, 4:19, 5:6 and 5:10. Daniel 2:29 matters for the question of origins: thoughts "came" to the king as he lay in bed.

1. The heart or mind is the place thoughts come from. Mark 7:21 and Matt 15:19 ("out of the heart come evil thoughts"). Also: "a heart that devises wicked plans" (Prov 6:18); "plan evil things in their heart" (Ps 140:2); "devise evil … in your heart" (Zech 7:10; 8:17); "The heart of man plans his way" (Prov 16:9); "his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy" (Isa 10:7); "the reasoning of their hearts" (Luke 9:47); In Jer 4:14, thoughts *lodge* within: "How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?" This follows the call to "wash your heart."

2. Thoughts arrive, often at night.: "as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be" (Dan 2:29); "thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men" (Job 4:13); "thoughts will come into your mind" (Ezek 38:10); "doubts arise in your hearts" (Luke 24:38); "an argument arose among them" (Luke 9:46); In Dan 2:29–30, the thoughts that come in the night are tied to revelation: "he who reveals mysteries made known to you."

3. The bed is also where people devise deliberately.: "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Ps 36:4); "devise wickedness … on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand" (Mic 2:1); The same place hosts thoughts that come unbidden (Dan 2:29) and thoughts that are worked on on purpose (Ps 36:4).
Against God: minds blinded by "the god of this world" (2 Cor 4:4), "his designs" (2 Cor 2:11), and "hearts were darkened" alongside futile thinking (Rom 1:21).

5. God is a thinker too, and his thinking has the last word. The same vocabulary is used of God: *maḥăšāvāh*: Jer 29:11; Ps 33:11; 40:5; 92:5; Isa 55:8–9; *ḥāšav*: Jer 18:11; 2 Sam 14:14; Lam 2:8; "the Lord takes thought for me" (Ps 40:17); "that you think of him" (Ps 144:3); *mᵊzimmāh*: "the intents of his heart" (Jer 23:20); "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2); In Gen 50:20 there are two opposite intentions about one event, expressed with the same verb: "you meant evil … God meant it for good." Human plans are real, but "it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand" (Prov 19:21; also Prov 16:9; Ps 33:10–11; Job 5:12).

9.2 What thoughts are: Design: forming something that does not yet exist. H2803G (19 rows) describes craftsmanship: cherubim "skillfully worked" (Exod 26:1, 31) and "skilled design" (Exod 39:3). The faculty itself is neutral. *Maḥăšāvāh* covers both artistry and plots, and *mᵊzimmāh* covers both "discretion" (Prov 2:11) and "evil devices" (Prov 12:2). What makes a thought good or evil is what it is designed toward.; Reckoning: giving something its value or category. H2803H/J (60 rows): Human misreckoning: Eli "took her to be a drunken woman" (1 Sam 1:13), "we esteemed him stricken" and "we esteemed him not" (Isa 53:3–4), Judah "thought she was a prostitute" (Gen 38:15).; God's reckoning: "he counted it to him as righteousness" (Gen 15:6), "the Lord counts no iniquity" (Ps 32:2), and the nations "accounted as the dust on the scales" (Isa 40:15, 17).; To think is to judge the worth of something, and people can judge wrongly.; Inner speech.; "all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Ps 10:4). The thought is quoted as a sentence.; Hannah "was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved" (1 Sam 1:13).; *Dialogismos* covers both inner reasoning and outward "argument", "quarreling" and "disputing".; "conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse" (Rom 2:15).; Something that affects the body and emotions.; "his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Dan 5:6; also 4:19; 5:10; 7:28).; "the cares of my heart" (Ps 94:19), and "haste within me" (Job 20:2).; A divided mind stalls a person: "limping between two different opinions" (1 Kgs 18:21, H5587A).; Creaturely and passing.; "but a breath" (Ps 94:11).; "When his breath departs … on that very day his plans perish" (Ps 146:4).; "futile" (1 Cor 3:20; Rom 1:21).; "striving of heart … striving after wind" (Eccl 2:22; 4:16).; Fully open to God.; "you discern my thoughts from afar" (Ps 139:2); also Ps 139:23; 1 Chr 28:9; "I know their works and their thoughts" (Isa 66:18); Heb 4:12.; Jesus knows people's thoughts (Luke 5:22; 6:8; 9:47; 11:17; Matt 9:4; 12:25).

9.3 From thought to action (Claude's reading): The verses trace a path from thought to deed: Arising. Thoughts come, often in the night (Dan 2:29; Job 4:13; Ezek 38:10; Luke 24:38).; Lodging. They stay and are dwelt on (Jer 4:14).; Reckoning. They weigh up and value things (Isa 53:4; 1 Sam 1:13).; Devising. They take the form of a plan (Ezek 38:10b; Ps 36:4).; Expression. Tongue, lips and eyes: "your tongue plots" (Ps 52:2), "devise words of deceit" (Ps 35:20), "winks his eyes plans" (Prov 16:30), "whisper … imagine the worst" (Ps 41:7).; Action. Hand and feet: "when the morning dawns, they perform it" (Mic 2:1); "a heart that devises … feet that make haste" (Prov 6:18); "their feet run to evil … their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity" (Isa 59:7).; The same path also runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Ps 119:59).

Where responsibility sits. The commands address the stages from lodging onward: "forsake … his thoughts" (Isa 55:7); "let none of you devise evil" (Zech 7:10); "take every thought captive" (2 Cor 10:5); "wash your heart" (Jer 4:14); The *arising* is not commanded, but it is not neutral either. What comes up shows the condition of the heart (Gen 6:5; Mark 7:21). So thoughts that arise reveal the heart, and devising engages the will. The heart itself can be changed from outside: written on, given discretion, guarded, or darkened.

2. Inward: outside influences → heart and mind.: God writes on minds and hearts (Heb 8:10; 10:16) and fills people with skill (Exod 35:35).; Instruction gives discretion (Prov 1:4).; Counsel establishes plans (Prov 15:22; 20:18).; The serpent leads thoughts astray (2 Cor 11:3), and "the god of this world" blinds (2 Cor 4:4).

3. Within: thoughts acting on the self.: "my thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me" (Job 20:2); "conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse" (Rom 2:15); "my thoughts greatly alarmed me" (Dan 7:28); "limping between two different opinions" (1 Kgs 18:21)
4. From thought into the body.: "his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Dan 5:6); "my color changed" (Dan 7:28)

6. Vertical: between God's thinking and human thinking.: God searches, knows and discerns thoughts (Ps 139:2, 23; 1 Chr 28:9; Heb 4:12).; God reckons (Gen 15:6; Ps 32:2).; God overrules: "you meant evil … God meant it for good" (Gen 50:20); "it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand" (Prov 19:21).; Human thought can also turn back toward God: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Ps 119:59).

3. New — not yet in any chapter: The path from thought to deed (§9.3). Arising (Dan 2:29; Job 4:13; Luk 24:38) → lodging (Jer 4:14) → reckoning (Isa 53:4) → devising (Ps 36:4) → expression through tongue, lips and eyes (Ps 52:2; Pro 16:30) → action through hand and feet (Mic 2:1; Pro 6:18; Isa 59:7). The same path runs toward good: "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Ps 119:59). Commands address the stages from lodging onward. Arising is not commanded, but it shows the state of the heart.; Thinking as reckoning, i.e. assigning worth (§9.2.2). Human misreckoning (Gen 38:15; 1Sa 1:13; Isa 53:3–4) against God's reckoning (Gen 15:6; Ps 32:2; Isa 40:15, 17). This links directly to justification language. It has no home in the narrative yet.; Thoughts that arrive, especially at night (§9.1.2–3). The bed is where thoughts come unbidden (Dan 2:29) and also where people plot on purpose (Ps 36:4; Mic 2:1). The night thoughts are tied to revelation (Dan 2:29–30).; Thought moves the body (§9.2.4). "his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way" (Dan 5:6); the divided mind "limping between two different opinions" (1Ki 18:21). This fits Ch 6 (flesh) or Ch 11 §3 ("The parts give way in sequence").; Outbound hearing: God hears the plots (§13.1). "You have heard their taunts … all their plots" (Lam 3:61); Mal 3:16. The narrative has hearing only as the inbound way in. Your comment in the discussion: *"Yes, hearing is an integral part of the outbound thought."*; Design and craft as the good form of devising (§9.2.1). Exod 26:1; 35:32–35: God fills craftsmen with skill "to devise artistic designs".

• enquiry (Ecc 1:16; 2:1, 15; 3:17–18; Deu 18:21; Jer 13:22)
• denial of God (Ps 14:1; 53:1)
